title: [Idea][Transport] Make authenticated WISP v2.1 usable from the WASM client
body:
## Problem and goal

Zeolite's server already has WISP v2.1 password/key authentication, but `docs/integration-guide.md` explicitly states the **shipped WASM WISP client sends no password/key credentials**. Consequently, deployments protecting `/wisp/` with the existing server authentication cannot use the direct WASM client and must route via an alternative relay or an unauthenticated endpoint.

Make the **existing WISP protocol authentication usable, documented and straightforward to configure** without inventing a new WebSocket protocol or leaking credentials to proxied sites. Feature request, not an assertion that the server's current auth implementation is broken.

## Proposed milestones

**1. Protocol/capability audit (required before implementation)**
- Verify the actual installed versions of the vendored libcurl/epoxy adapters, `wisp-core` and `wisp_extensions`; document what WISP v2.1 password/key auth extensions the client can negotiate in-browser and which modes require upstream vendor support or a small adapter.
- Confirm server/client interoperability against `zeolite_server::wisp_handler` with a real authenticated session. Do not assume HTTP `Authorization` is injectable from native browser WebSocket (it generally isn't), and never put credentials in URL, query strings, subprotocol tokens or diagnostic events.
- Preserve WISP v2.1 stream multiplexing and retry semantics.

**2. Host-authorized credential configuration**
- Provide a typed **host-only** control-plane/configuration seam for `none`, `password` and (where actually supported) `ed25519` / key identity mode. Include credential identity/mode, selected endpoint, capability and connection status; keep the secret payload outside `zl:ping`, DevTools, ordinary KDL files and browser-visible shim globals.
- Credentials should be session-scoped where possible, memory-only by default, rotated/cleared on disconnect/log-out/teardown and never inherited by a different virtual site, browser tab or host. If a host offers storage, require a separate deliberate secure-storage design; do not persist plaintext passwords or private keys to CacheStorage, logs, KDL or `localStorage`.
- Fail closed for missing/partial/malformed credentials. No unauthenticated downgrade *after* auth is configured unless the host explicitly opts into an alternative relay; never silently switch to a public WISP endpoint.
- WSS/TLS by default for credentialed endpoints; explicit reject or warn on `ws://` with secrets.

**3. Real handshake and errors**
- Implement vendor-compatible client authentication; return stable, redacted statuses (`auth-unsupported`, `auth-required`, `invalid-credential`, `expired/rotated`, `connection-failed`, `unknown`). Do not misreport an upstream network error as rejected credentials.
- Test both primary/alternate WISP routing, worker restart, concurrent streams, failure/reconnect and no accidental credential replay to other endpoints.
- Authentication handshake logs must never expose raw password/proof/signature/key bytes. Surface codes/evidence into #494 KDL debugger and the `zl:doctor` report instead.
- Keep the existing relay transport available where WISP authentication is unsupported.

**4. Documentation and host ergonomics**
- End-to-end standalone Zeolite setup: how to configure authenticated `zeolite-server`, provide host-side credentials, connect and verify successful authenticated WISP (plus troubleshooting).
- Suggested host UI (e.g. LobsterBrowse Settings): WISP endpoint, authentication mode, account/identity, connection test, credential replacement and disconnect, plus clear privacy warnings; no secrets displayed after save.

## Acceptance

- A real browser + real Zeolite server test opens a WISP session requiring password auth and successfully fetches a fixture; a missing/incorrect credential is denied. Test key auth only when the client supports it.
- Negative/abuse tests cover origin allowlist, rate limits, endpoint-switch secret isolation, reconnect, key rotation, invalid credentials, mixed auth extensions and auth downgrade.
- No credentials, secret-derived values or challenge proof are visible to proxied JS, workers, `zl:ping`, KDL export (#494), doctor or MCP output. Raw secrets must not appear in browser navigation/network URLs.
- The shipped default remains functional on supported unauthenticated endpoints; unsupported auth configurations fail explicitly without opening an unintended relay.
- Documentation and tests replace the current 'cannot send password/key credentials' limitation **only after actual browser + server interoperability is verified**.

Related: #494 (redacted diagnostics), prior transport #168/#154, `docs/integration-guide.md`, `docs/security.md`.

title: add plan as a PR (never merged)
body:
# Project: Browser-based P2P "social proxy" for a pair of peers

## Goal
Two users (a pair), each partially restricted (e.g. China <-> outside), browse via
each other's connection, both directions at the same time. No operated exit servers.
Setup servers are OK (STUN/WSS/MQTT/Nostr/manual). First target: China.
Scalability beyond 2 peers is future work.

## Decisions
- Web app + browser only. No native helper, no new browser (revisit on evidence).
- Client = plain web app (any modern browser). Host = small WebExtension,
  because of CORS/SOP: page code can't read arbitrary cross-origin responses,
  and WebSocket/WebRTC can't reach arbitrary sites. Only an extension
  (host_permissions) or a WS->TCP gateway can be an exit.
- Extension priority: Chromium MV3 (Chrome/Edge/Brave) > Firefox > Safari (Client-only).
- Exit sees plaintext (social trust, not anonymity). Host IP is origin (liability).

## Architecture
- Node module, container-agnostic (Chromium offscreen doc reason WEB_RTC /
  Firefox event page / plain page): signaling adapters, transport manager,
  AEAD frames, mux, exit adapter.
- Pairing: 128-bit secret in URL fragment/QR; HKDF -> room id, signaling key,
  session keys. AES-GCM (WebCrypto). SDP sealed; DTLS fingerprint pinned.
- Signaling adapters: manual QR/text; own WSS relay; MQTT over WSS
  (public brokers, e.g. broker-cn.emqx.io); Nostr relays.
- Data transports: WebRTC DataChannel (primary); WSS relay fallback
  (required: CGNAT/symmetric NAT); TURNS:443 optional; WebTransport later
  (GFW does SNI-based QUIC blocking since Apr 2024).
- Mux (HTTP-level): OPEN, BODY, RESP_HEAD, RESP_BODY, END, RST, WINDOW;
  16 KiB frames, credit flow control, stream-id parity (A odd, B even).
- Exit adapters: fetch-ext (v1); ws-exit (Wisp/Snowflake-style, later); native (later).
- Extension = stateless fetch executor: optional host_permissions,
  credentials:'omit', DNR session rules for Cookie/Referer/Origin,
  webRequest observe for Set-Cookie, SSRF guard (RFC1918/loopback/link-local,
  re-check after DNS), ports 80/443, follow redirects and report final URL.
- Client rendering: Service Worker at /~/<enc-url> + URL/JS rewriting
  (Scramjet/Ultraviolet, check AGPL); sandboxed iframes; keys in isolated worker.
- Symmetric roles: each peer is Client + Host (host_enabled flag),
  reachability probes -> capability advert -> per-domain "via peer" routing.
- Background: Chromium offscreen doc (no lifetime limit except audio);
  strict-web: pinned tab (real-time connections are exempt from timer
  throttling), Memory Saver exception, no timer-driven pumps; handle
  sleep/wake with ICE restart + transport fallback. Mobile = foreground Client only.

## Threats (China)
IP/port blocking (STUN, signaling, peer IPs); SNI/DNS blocking of
signaling/relay domains; UDP/DTLS fingerprinting/throttling; QUIC SNI blocking;
malicious signaling server (AEAD); endpoint/legal risk. A static pair has no
pool for resilience (unlike Snowflake) -> fallbacks matter.

## Prior art
Snowflake (stranger pool, operated bridges, WebRTC->WS), uProxy (friend-to-friend
extension, discontinued), Flashproxy, Lantern Unbounded, Wisp/epoxy-tls,
Ultraviolet/Scramjet.

## Plan
1. M0 (1-2 wk): diagnostics page (STUN/WSS/MQTT/QUIC reachability, NAT type)
   + hidden-tab/offscreen soak test, run from 2 real China networks.
   Gate 1: P2P success rate -> relay investment. Gate 2: can the in-China
   peer install the extension?
2. M1: pairing, signaling adapters, WebRTC + WSS relay, encrypted frames.
3. M2: mux + extension exit, SSRF guard, headless Host in offscreen doc.
4. M3: Service Worker rewriting; 20-site corpus per direction.
5. M4: transport manager, sleep/wake recovery, STUN health checks.
6. M5: bidirectional UX, routing rules, consent, threat-model review.
7. Later: desktop wrapper with SOCKS, ws-exit pool, browser fork only if
   measured evidence demands it.

## To verify in M0
Firefox event-page survival with open WebRTC; fetch from offscreen doc with
host_permissions; mainland-reachable STUN list; extension install path in
China (store access vs sideload); chrome-vs-firefox WebRTC interop matrix.

## Start here
Implement M0: diagnostics page + signaling adapter interface + two-tab
manual-SDP WebRTC echo/throughput test.

title: Add opt-in SFU voice and screen forwarding for the Astana VPS
body:
Wisp currently uploads a copy of voice and screen media to each participant. Add opt-in SFU mode: one native SIPSorcery uplink per user, source-bound downlinks, and a small Go/Pion Linux service forwarding Opus/H.264 and existing SCTP channels without transcoding.

The service verifies Firebase ID tokens, membership, voice-channel type and owned fresh seats; independently caps rooms at five and rejects duplicate sessions. WSS requires an unexpired pinned certificate. Existing Firebase rules/presence and default P2P remain supported, with no silent fallback or TURN deployment. SDP/ICE ordering, bounded candidate queues and retired-connection history handle delayed answers and room churn.

Includes a constrained systemd service, repeatable Ubuntu amd64 installer for 89.126.195.20, dependency notices and docs/SFU.md covering setup, bandwidth, certificate rotation and limits. No VPS deployment or production Firebase writes were performed.

Validation on final commit 96cbecc: Windows CI passed 78 core + 10 desktop tests with no skips, resource validation and build/publish/package. title: Fixing Netlify deploy error by updating expo command in build script
body:
🔗 **View agent run:** https://app.netlify.com/projects/reliable-llama-0bea30/agent-runs/6adebc2051a8d23769ec61ee

🤖 **Agent:** Claude (claude-opus-5-5)

💬 **Prompt:** The Netlify deploy errored, with the following guidance provided:

The build fails at [line 97](#L97) because the `expo` CLI command is not found in the system PATH.

This typically happens when the build command uses `expo` directly instead of invok...

✅ **Result:** The Netlify deploy first failed because the dashboard build command was `expo export -p web`, but this project isn't an Expo app. Once that command was replaced, the site's own build failed too: a recent commit had moved the `assets/` folder from `static/assets/` to the repository root, and the build no longer found it. The obfuscating build was updated to read from the new location.

That build was still the wrong fit for Netlify. It randomizes page and file paths and relies on the project's Express server to map them back, so on static hosting the home page showed only a broken search box and the Apps, Games, Tabs and Settings links didn't work. Netlify now uses a separate static build (`pnpm run build:static`). It publishes the root `index.html` unchanged, the other pages from `static/`, the root `assets/` folder, and the proxy libraries (Ultraviolet, Scramjet, bare-mux, Epoxy, libcurl) at the same paths the local dev server uses. Pages are served at their normal routes. Because `index.html` sets `<base href="/solana/">`, a rewrite sends `/solana/*` requests to the site root so relative links and scripts still load. The original obfuscating build and the Express server were not changed apart from the asset-path fix.

The proxy also needs a Wisp server, which is a WebSocket backend. Netlify Functions can't run WebSocket servers, so it has to be hosted elsewhere, for example by running this repo's Node server on a host that supports it. Its address can be entered on the site's Settings page, or set as a `WISP_URL` environment variable (for example `wss://your-server.example/wisp/`) to make it the default for every visitor. Without one, the pages load but browsing through the proxy won't work. Server-only features such as analytics, the GitHub games endpoint and password protection also don't run on static hosting.

title: v86: real emulator-side networking + the networking.sh script
body:
## `networking.sh`

Shipped as `public/v86/scripts/networking.sh`, installed at `/root/networking.sh` in the initramfs, and copied into the OS filesystem at `~/v86/root/networking.sh` so you can read and edit it in Files. The full Arch guest sees it at `/root/networking.sh` too.

It does the same job as the script in copy.sh's images (upstream wires one at `/root/networking.sh` in its Dockerfiles, and issue #528 points people at `./networking.sh` in the Arch profile): load the NIC driver, take a lease, done. Ours also handles the static address, writes `/etc/resolv.conf`, and adds `status` / `down` / `static` modes.

## The emulator side

Networking is not something the guest can arrange for itself, so this was mostly emulator work:

```js
net_device: { type: "virtio", relay_url: "wss://relay.widgetry.org/" }
```

- v86 emulates the **virtio-net card** → guest sees `eth0`
- the **backend answers DHCP** for its local link → `192.168.86.100`, router/DNS `192.168.86.1`
- traffic beyond that link goes **through the relay**

Settings → **v86 network** takes the relay URL, picked by scheme:

| URL | Backend | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `wss://relay.widgetry.org/` (default) | wsproxy | nothing — copy.sh's own public relay |
| `wisp://your-server:port` | wisp | your own proxy |
| `fetch` | in-page stack | nothing, but CORS limits what it can reach |
| `off` | none | guest gets loopback only |

**Settings → Test** opens the exact socket the emulator will open and reports what happened. That matters because a dead relay looks *identical* to a broken guest from inside the VM: the interface comes up, `networking.sh` runs, and the lease simply never arrives.

## Verified — real guest, real proxy

I ran a wisp proxy locally and booted the actual kernel against it:

```
[PASS] interface exists in guest
[PASS] DHCP lease from v86's backend
[PASS] default route via the emulated router
[PASS] DNS configured
[PASS] networking.sh reports success
[PASS] no DHCP failure fallback
[PASS] real TCP traffic through the emulated NIC   ← HTTP GET returned from the host
```

That last line is the one that matters: a plain HTTP request left the guest through the emulated NIC and came back with real content.

Without a relay, the same boot loads `virtio_net`, shows `eth0`, and times out on DHCP — reproduced, and the reason the probe exists.

`npm run build` passes (tsc + CSS guard + worker test + vite). Stamp **0.9.0**.

## Phone test

Settings → v86 network → **Test**. Expect *"relay reachable (wsproxy)"*. Then Terminal → Reconnect, and in the guest:

```sh
/root/networking.sh        # loads the driver, takes a lease, prints status
ping -c 2 192.168.86.1     # the emulated router answers
```

If Test fails, the relay is blocked on your network — paste me the red line and I'll point the default somewhere better (a self-hosted wisp URL works with the same setting).

title: Duplicate relays (host and host:443) in nostr_relays.csv waste geohash relay slots — 48 of 388 entries affected
body:
## Summary

`nostr_relays.csv` lists many relays twice, once as `host` and once as `host:443`. Bitchat normalizes entries only by prefixing `wss://`, so both survive as distinct relays and can both land in the 5 nearest-relay slots for a geohash. Users then get fewer real relays than intended, and sometimes one of the two forms doesn't even work.

## Scope

In today's list (commit from 2026-10-23 07:03 UTC), **48 of 388 relays (~12%)** appear in both forms after normalizing `:443`, e.g. `nos.lol`, `vault.iris.to`, `relay.gulugulu.moe`, `chat-relay.zap-work.com`, `nostr.stakey.net`, `relay.wisp.talk`, `nostr.snowbla.de`.

## Real-world impact: `u0` (France) during the current surge

Bitchat is currently **#1 overall in the French App Store**, so `u0` is busy. Its 5 relays (nearest to the cell center 47.81, 5.63) are:

| # | Relay | Distance | Status (2026-10-23) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | wss://relay.artio.inf.unibe.ch | 167 km | ✅ up |
| 2 | wss://nostr.sathoarder.com:443 | 179 km | ✅ up |
| 3 | wss://nostr.sathoarder.com | 179 km | ❌ HTTP 500 / timeouts (same server as #2) |
| 4 | wss://test-relay.uid.ovh | 179 km | ✅ up |
| 5 | wss://nostr.unkn0wn.world | 198 km | ✅ up |

So all of France's geohash traffic rides on **4 physical relays with one dead slot**, including one named `test-relay`. Interestingly, the bare-host form of sathoarder fails while the `:443` form works, so dedup should keep the form that passes the health check.

## Suggested fixes

**georelays (data):**
1. Normalize URLs before writing the CSV: lowercase the host, strip the default port (`:443` for wss, `:80` for ws), strip trailing `/`.
2. When both forms exist, keep the one that passed the connectivity test (or prefer the bare host if both pass).
3. Optionally, add a CI check that fails if normalized duplicates exist.

**bitchat-android / bitchat (iOS), defense in depth:**
- In `RelayDirectory.normalizeRelayUrl()` (Android) and the iOS equivalent, strip default ports and dedupe *before* `closestRelaysForGeohash()` takes the top N, so a bad list can't eat slots.
- Consider skipping relays that failed to connect recently when picking the N nearest, so a dead relay doesn't permanently hold a slot for a whole region.

## How to reproduce

- Download `nostr_relays.csv`, normalize the hosts (strip `:443`), and count the duplicates: 48.
- Decode geohash `u0` to its center, sort the relays by distance, and take the top 5: the list above.
- `nak req -k 20000 -l 1 wss://nostr.sathoarder.com` fails, while `wss://nostr.sathoarder.com:443` returns events.

title: Rebuild as 0.9.1:1 for the updated Debian certificate store
body:
Rebuilds the package as `0.9.1:1` so the image picks up Debian's `ca-certificates 20250419~deb12u2`, released to bookworm on 2026-10-20. That update removes the Sectigo `AAA Certificate Services` and `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` roots, which are the anchors for the eMudhra intermediate CAs whose private keys were compromised.

`0.9.1:0` was built on 2026-10-08 with `deb12u1`. Wisp's TLS on Linux trusts the system bundle and does no revocation checking, so in that build Spider Sync would accept a certificate for an upstream relay issued by one of the compromised intermediates. Event signatures still prevent forged events, but a man in the middle could withhold events or observe sync traffic.

The only change is the version and one added sentence in each locale of the release notes. The Dockerfile already installs `ca-certificates` from bookworm at build time, so a fresh build gets the fix.

Verified on a fresh x86_64 build of this branch (`docker build --pull --no-cache`):

- `dpkg-query -W ca-certificates` reports `20250419~deb12u2` (148 roots).
- `openssl verify -CAfile` against the image's `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` rejects all 16 compromised intermediates (8 emSign-issued, 8 Sectigo cross-signed). The same check against a `deb12u1` bundle accepts the 8 cross-signed ones.
- The relay starts as `wisp` (uid 999), serves NIP-11 reporting 0.9.1, and Spider Sync completes TLS to `wss://relay.damus.io` and fetches events.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` and the SDK's Prettier check pass.

title: Custom WISP server only affects a secondary route; normal browsing ignores it
body:
## Problem

Settings > WISP servers lets users add their own `wss://` WISP server (for example `wss://anura.pro`), but the choice does not carry normal browsing:

- The primary transport uses `ZL_WISP_URL` from the Zeolite bundle (`app/src/config.ts`), a build-time constant. The user's selection never reaches it.
- The selection is announced only through `zl:wispRegister`, which feeds the secondary policy route `wisp`. The engine picks that route per host, only for hosts that refuse the relay class.
- The result: adding a server changes almost nothing for typical sites, while the UI copy says the active server "sees every destination you visit and relays your traffic". That copy is wrong today.
- The field is on `main` but missing from `beta/zeolite-nativetransit`, which is the branch that serves the beta deployment.

## Proposed fix (option 1: the active server carries all traffic)

1. Zeolite: a runtime setter for the primary WISP URL (for example `zl:wispPrimary`). It replaces the constant in the primary transport, re-initialises the libcurl and wisp clients, and persists with the route shape like `zl:wispRegister` does. An empty value restores `ZL_WISP_URL`.
2. LobsterBrowse beta: port the WISP server list, selector, ping and delete UI from `main`. The active server is sent to the engine at boot and on every change.
3. Pin bump to the Zeolite commit that carries (1). Verify the served `/zlsw/bootstrap.js` hash after deploy.

## Acceptance

- With a custom server active, a fresh navigation's primary transport connects to that server (check the WebSocket URL in the network log).
- With "LobsterBrowse server (default)" selected, behaviour matches today.
- Password-protected servers still fail with an honest error, as the current copy says.

## Notes

- The server sees all destinations you visit. The UI should say so.
- Not verified: that `wss://anura.pro` is a working WISP endpoint. Test with the Ping button before relying on it.

title: feat(app): runtime primary WISP endpoint (zl:wispPrimary)
body:
## Summary

Adds `zl:wispPrimary`: the embedder can change the primary transport's WISP endpoint at runtime. Until now `ZL_WISP_URL` was a build-time constant, so a host app could only add a secondary per-host route.

- `config.ts`: `normalizeWispUrl` (ws/wss only, never throws), `primaryWispUrl()`, runtime override state.
- `transport.ts`: `setPrimaryWisp(url)` swaps the endpoint and resets the libcurl client. An invalid URL is refused with no change. `""` restores `ZL_WISP_URL`.
- `control.ts`: the `zl:wispPrimary` message, persisted with the route shape.
- `request.ts`: `wisp-primary` is written to and restored from the saved route, so a restarted worker keeps the choice.

title: [Feature][Settings] Custom wss:// WISP servers with ping, LobsterBrowse server always selectable
body:
Add a custom `wss://` WISP server option that shows its ping, and always keep the LobsterBrowse server selectable with its ping.

**What exists today**

- The engine already takes a WISP URL at init (`zlWispInit(wispUrl)` in `App.tsx`), so the plumbing for a non-default server is there.
- #128 (closed) showed that `/build` publishes `SCRAMJET_WISP_URL` and bypasses the `/wisp/` password. Any custom-server feature must not reopen that path.

**Proposed approach**

1. Settings: a list of WISP servers (name, `wss://` URL). Only `wss://` is accepted, except `ws://localhost` for dev. The LobsterBrowse server is always in the list, marked as default and not deletable.
2. Ping: open a WebSocket to each entry on demand, time the open, close it, show ms. Do not ping on every page load.
3. Selecting a server calls the engine's WISP init with that URL. Show a warning that the chosen server sees every destination you visit.
4. Credentials for password-protected servers: stored only in the session, never in the built bundle.

**Open questions**

- Whether the engine's wisp endpoint needs a version handshake (`zl:ping` is per-worker, not per-server).
- What happens to the active tabs when the server is switched (reload all, or only new tabs).
- Ping is an open-to-open timing, not ICMP. Label it that way.

**Acceptance**

- Ping shows for the LobsterBrowse server and for a custom server.
- A custom server that does not answer shows "unreachable", not a hang.
- No credential appears in `/build` output or in the bundle.

title: Why can't access websites like TikTok
body:
🔗 **View agent run:** https://app.netlify.com/projects/quiet-monstera-7531c7/agent-runs/6ad7b5bcb9330e9129d83987

🤖 **Agent:** Claude

💬 **Prompt:** 为什么无法访问网站，如tiktok

✅ **Result:** Sites such as TikTok couldn't be opened through the proxy on the Netlify deployment. The homepage loaded fine, but the actual web proxy (Ultraviolet and Scramjet) sends every page it fetches through a WebSocket connection to a "wisp" server at `/wisp/` on the current site. Netlify Edge Functions can't relay WebSocket connections, so on this site `/wisp/` returned a normal web page instead of opening a tunnel. Every proxied site therefore failed to load.

lunaar.org's own wisp server does accept WebSocket connections from this domain (a test handshake succeeded). The Netlify edge function now rewrites the proxy scripts as they pass through, so they connect straight to `wss://lunaar.org/wisp/` rather than this site's `/wisp/`. Everything else is still served through this site. When tested locally with Netlify's dev server, both proxy scripts showed the new wisp address and the homepage still loaded.

Notes:
- Proxied traffic now goes directly between the visitor's browser and lunaar.org. If a network blocks lunaar.org itself, the proxy fails there too. Avoiding that would mean hosting your own wisp server somewhere that supports WebSockets, such as the existing Render setup.
- The "bare" transport option in Lunaar's settings still points at this site and may not work fully. The default transport (libcurl) and epoxy both use wisp.
- Browsers that visited the site before may need a hard refresh, or their site data cleared, so they load the updated scripts.
- Some sites, TikTok in particular, use heavy anti-bot checks and may still load partly or not at all through any web proxy.

body:
## Browser app (Scramjet)

Cloned MercuryWorkshop/scramjet and studied its build. The full source build requires a Rust/wasm toolchain (and the demo app drags in Monaco etc.), so this vendors the **published npm builds of the exact versions the repo pins**, plus our own lean browser front end:

- `public/scramjet/` deploys to `https://dragon-gaming-platforms.github.io/Dragon86/scramjet/`
  - `@mercuryworkshop/scramjet@2.0.67-alpha.2`, `scramjet-controller@0.0.14`, `epoxy-transport@3.0.1`, `libcurl-transport@2.0.5`, `scramjet-utils@0.0.3` (file-by-file map in `public/scramjet/VENDORED.md`, AGPL-3.0 text included)
  - **Path corrections**: the upstream demo hardcodes site-root paths (`/scramjet/scramjet.js`, `/controller/controller.sw.js`, prefix `/~/sj/`). Every path (sw.js import, controller `prefix`/`scramjetPath`/`injectPath`/`wasmPath`) is now computed from the page's own directory, so it works under `/Dragon86/scramjet/`
  - Own minimal UI: address bar (URL or DuckDuckGo search), back/forward/reload/home, settings panel for Wisp server + transport (Epoxy/Libcurl), persisted to localStorage, `[D86:browser]` console logs
  - Default Wisp endpoint is the one the upstream demo builds against (`wss://anura.pro/`) — GitHub Pages can't host a Wisp server; all proxy traffic flows through it, so it's user-configurable
- New **Browser** app in Dragon86 (globe icon, desktop + taskbar) that iframes the deployed `/Dragon86/scramjet/` URL, with Reload and Open-standalone toolbar actions

## Cache service worker (as a layer — read why)

Requested: a second SW forcing cache-first for everything except the hoster. **Browsers allow only one service worker per scope**, so a separate registration at `/Dragon86/` would replace/fight the COI worker. The cache therefore lives as a layer inside the existing worker (documented in its banner): cache-first stale-while-revalidate for static assets (script/style/image/font/worker), **excluding any CheerpX-Bridge URL and the whole `/scramjet/` subtree** (dynamic proxy traffic must never be frozen into cache), navigations never cached. Hoster stays live-network, always.

## Verification (sandbox has no browser)

- `npm run build` passes; all 13 Scramjet asset paths return 200 from the production build preview
- JS syntax-checked (`node --check`), controller/runtime versions pinned to the matching pair the controller asserts at startup

## Test checklist (needs a real browser)

- [ ] Open **Browser** from the desktop — Scramjet page loads inside the window, status reaches "Ready."
- [ ] Type `example.com` — page renders proxied; try a search term — DuckDuckGo results
- [ ] Click links inside a proxied page — navigation stays inside the proxy (URL bar follows)
- [ ] Settings panel: switch transport Epoxy/Libcurl, Save & reconnect — still browses
- [ ] Terminal still connects (embedded) — cache layer didn't freeze the hoster; second visit loads OS assets from cache

> AGPL note: Scramjet is AGPL-3.0 — the vendored copy carries its license, but the org should keep the corresponding-source story in mind for the deployed site.

title: Vendor GUST + Sandstone apps; Monaco editor
body:
Three requested additions, all vendored locally (no CDNs at runtime):

**GUST (web proxy)** — cloned `nautilus-os/GUST`, took its single-file app, and downloaded everything it used to fetch from CDNs so it loads completely self-contained: Google Fonts → local font files (npm `@fontsource`), Font Awesome → local copy (official GitHub release), the `iso-639-1` script → local copy (npm). Its proxy engine was already built into the file. Added as a desktop/start-menu app.

**Sandstone (web proxy)** — cloned `ading2210/sandstone`, built it from source here (its engine's wasm ends up inside its JS bundle, so there was no separate CDN file to fetch), and vendored the built example frontend. Added as a desktop/start-menu app. Note: Sandstone talks to a *Wisp server* over websocket (default `wss://wisp.mercurywork.shop/`, changeable in its Options) — that's a live service, not a downloadable file.

**Monaco Editor** — downloaded `monaco-editor` (0.57.0, latest) from the npm registry and vendored its minified build. The Text Editor now opens text/code files in Monaco (the editor from VS Code): syntax highlighting by file type, dark theme, Ctrl+S still saves. If Monaco ever fails to load, the old plain editor stays as a fallback.

All licenses are included next to each vendored copy (GUST/Sandstone are AGPL, Monaco is MIT).

## Please test on your phone
1. Two new desktop icons: **GUST** and **Sandstone** — open each, try loading a website in both. (Sandstone: if nothing loads, check its Options → Wisp URL is `wss://wisp.mercurywork.shop/`.)
2. Open **Text Editor**, create/open a code file (e.g. name it `test.js` in Files, then open it) — you should get colored syntax highlighting; edit something, Ctrl+S (or Save), reopen, and confirm your change stuck.
3. Quick sanity: Scramjet, Dragon Gaming Platforms, Files, Terminal still open fine.

title: Upgrade proxies for functionality
body:
🔗 **View agent run:** https://app.netlify.com/projects/lucent-cassata-2453e4/agent-runs/6ad5e99c9383a0b4332f1032

🤖 **Agent:** Claude

💬 **Prompt:** upgrade the proxies on here so it actually works

✅ **Result:** The web proxies in NautilusOS (the Ultraviolet app, the built-in Browser, the VS Code app and custom web apps) now load sites again. They had stopped working for a few reasons, all of which were fixed.

**Dead proxy servers.** Both default Wisp servers had gone offline: `wisp.rhw.one` times out and `construction.services.codd70.ru` no longer resolves. The new default is `wss://wisp.mercurywork.shop/`, which responds. Anyone who still has one of the old dead addresses saved in their settings is moved to the new default automatically. The Ultraviolet app also had its server hardcoded, so it ignored the Wisp setting. It now uses the URL from Settings › Network, and changing that setting takes effect right away without a reload.

**Updated proxy libraries.** bare-mux went from 2.1.7 to 2.1.9, and the libcurl transport from 1.5.0 to 1.5.2 (which brings libcurl.js from 0.7.1 to 0.7.4). Ultraviolet was already on the latest release (3.2.10). The newer 2.x/3.x transport packages need a different system that Ultraviolet doesn't support, so the latest versions that work with Ultraviolet were used.

**Startup timing.** Pages could request a proxied URL before the proxy's service worker was running, and the server answered with a 404. Proxy setup (service worker plus transport) now lives in one shared script, `js/proxy.js`, and every navigation waits for it to finish. A fallback was also added for URLs that load before the proxy is running, such as when the VS Code app first opens, a custom web app launches, or someone hard-refreshes. In those cases a small page starts the proxy and reloads, so the site appears instead of a 404.

**Built-in Browser.** The Browser app sent pages through a third-party CORS service and pasted the raw HTML into the window. That broke most sites, and the code then crashed on a missing iframe. It now opens pages through Ultraviolet in an iframe, like the Ultraviolet app. An inline script in `index.html` that crashed on every page load was also removed.

All of this was tested in a headless browser against the local dev server. The Ultraviolet app, the built-in Browser and a direct proxied URL in a fresh browser all loaded example.com through the new Wisp server, with no page errors.

One thing to keep in mind: the site depends on a free public Wisp server it doesn't control, and Netlify can't host one because it doesn't support long-lived WebSocket connections. If `wisp.mercurywork.shop` goes down, users can enter another server in Settings › Network. For long-term reliability, it's worth running your own Wisp server elsewhere and making it the default.

title: [App Submission] Pi Browser Agnet
body:
### App Name

Pi Browser Agnet

### App Description

# Pollinations APP Submission — Quest #15923

## PR Description

This USES **Pi in the Browser** under `apps/pi-browser` — the **real Pi coding agent** (the unmodified `pi` CLI v0.87.1 by earendil-works, loaded from the Wasmer registry as `wasmer/pi@=0.87.1`) running **entirely client-side** in a WebAssembly sandbox. There is no Pi-inspired reimplementation and no remote agent — the actual Pi binary executes in the page via the Wasmer SDK (WASIX + Web Workers), and every model call is paid with the visitor's own Pollen through **Bring Your Own Pollen**.

### What was used

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Pi agent** | `wasmer/pi@=0.87.1` from the Wasmer registry — the real Pi CLI running on Edge.js inside WASIX, with its bundled bash, coreutils, fd, ripgrep, grep, sed, findutils |
| **Wasmer SDK** | `@wasmer/sdk` 0.19.0 (`@wasmer/sdk/browser`) — sandbox creation, package loading with progress, filesystem access, process spawning. Vendored at install time (postinstall) so the SDK's worker/wasm URL resolution is untouched by bundlers |
| **BYO Pollen** | OAuth authorization-code flow **with PKCE** from `BRING_YOUR_OWN_POLLEN.md` — the user authorizes the app at `enter.pollinations.ai`, the app exchanges the code browser-side (PKCE, no secret), and the returned `sk_...` key is kept in memory/`sessionStorage` only |
| **Models** | `GET gen.pollinations.ai/v1` → tool-calling models fetched live; the chosen model is injected into the sandbox's `models.json` as an `openai-completions` provider with `baseUrl: https://gen.pollinations.ai/v1` — Pi speaks to Pollinations exactly like any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Switching models mid-session rewrites `models.json` live |
| **Network** | Browsers can't open TCP sockets, so Pi's HTTPS traffic is tunneled through a **WISP** server the visitor controls: one-click deploy of `wasmer/wisp-server` to a free Wasmer account (auto-configures the tab), a local `wasmer run wasmer/wisp-server --net`, or any `wss://` endpoint |
| **Automation** | Each message runs `pi --mode json --offline --provider pollinations --model <id> --tools read,write,edit,bash,grep,find,ls --session-id <id> "<prompt>"`; the app consumes Pi's JSONL event stream (streaming text, thinking, tool calls) and renders it live. Conversation continuity via Pi sessions inside the sandbox |

### How the app flow works

1. **Connect** — visitor clicks *Connect Pollinations account* → PKCE OAuth → their key + Pollen balance shown (they choose their own budget on the consent screen). An `sk_...` key can also be pasted directly.
2. **Pick a model** — live list of tool-calling Pollinations models with context size and Pollen pricing per million tokens.
3. **Network tunnel (WISP)** — one-click Wasmer deploy / local CLI / custom `wss://` URL. Can also be deferred; the app asks the first time Pi needs the network.
4. **Launch** — the app downloads `wasmer/pi@=0.87.1` (cached in browser storage afterwards) and boots a WASIX sandbox with an in-memory workspace seeded with a small starter project, plus `.pi/models.json`, `.pi/auth.json`, and an `APPEND_SYSTEM.md` that tells Pi about its browser environment.
5. **Work** — the visitor prompts Pi in a chat panel; Pi's text streams token-by-token, tool calls appear as live cards (bash command + output, file writes/edits), and the **workspace file tree updates live** with a built-in file viewer. Users can switch models, cancel runs, start fresh conversations, or restart the sandbox.

### App URL

https://pi-browser-agent.namansoni.in/

### GitHub Repository URL

https://github.com/NamanSoni78/pi-browser-agent

bots

en

title: Consolidated: WISP binary protocol, player auto-source, Turnstile, cleanup
body:
## Summary

Consolidates all three outstanding PRs into one:

**From #3 — WISP worker**
- Rewrote `wisp-worker/src/wisp.ts` to the **binary Wisp protocol v1/v2** per the official spec (MercuryWorkshop/wisp-protocol), replacing the custom JSON dialect
- Packet format `type(u8) + streamID(u32 LE) + payload`; client-chosen stream IDs; initial CONTINUE handshake; INFO handshake for v2 clients; spec close-reason codes; per-stream FIFO buffering
- Fixed binary WebSocket frame handling (`event.data` arrives as Blob in workerd)
- Migrated Durable Object to SQLite backing (`new_sqlite_classes`) — required by Cloudflare error 10099
- `WISP_SOCKS5` secret set with 18 IPVanish endpoints, random rotation + failover

**From #4 — Movie player**
- `playSource` now waits for the video element to actually deliver data before accepting a source, so the auto-source loop only stops on a URL that genuinely plays
- Mid-playback failures auto-switch to the next source
- Turnstile enforced: `TURNSTILE_SECRET` set on the main worker

**From #5 — Cleanup**
- Anime page loads a single merged `anime.js` (seed catalogs + app code)
- Removed ~2,400 lines of dead weight: stale anime duplicates, dead `hub.css`, unreferenced data JSON artifacts
- Agents terminal now uses our own WISP worker (`wss://goarxyz-wisp.goarxyz.workers.dev/wisp`) instead of third-party `wisp.mercurywork.shop`

## Verification (all live on goar.app / goarxyz-wisp worker)
- WISP: 5/5 SSH streams through rotating SOCKS5; IRC banner via 6667; multiplexed streams OK
- Turnstile: 403 without/with fake token; 200 with valid flow
- Player: new `waitForMedia`/`videoRecovery` logic live in watch.js
- Cleanup: deleted paths 404; anime page single-script; agents page own-wisp only
- `tsc --noEmit` clean; `node --check` clean on all touched JS

title: UDP egress on the default relay (linuxontab-net)
body:
Follow-up to #7 / #15. WispSlirp now speaks Wisp v2 and opens UDP streams when the backend advertises the UDP extension, and the default relay `wss://linuxontab-net.fly.dev/wisp` negotiates v2 — but TCP only: its INFO carries no extensions and UDP CONNECTs are refused with 0x41, which the guest sees as ICMP port-unreachable. So on the default path there is still no QUIC, NTP, WireGuard, or DNS to a resolver of the guest's choosing (DoH/DNS-over-TCP remain the DNS routes).

**Goal:** the relay advertises the UDP extension (`0x01`) in INFO and carries UDP streams: one `tokio::net::UdpSocket` per stream, one Wisp DATA frame per datagram in each direction, idle streams closed, and refusals (blocked ports, unresolvable hosts) reported with a CLOSE reason so the guest gets a clean unreachable rather than a timeout.

Where: `traits/sys/serve/wisp.rs` in the traits.build repo, deployed from branch `wisp-v2-on-may14` — see `services/wisp-backend/README.md` for the pinned-branch build and the canary smoke test (building from traits.build `main` crash-loops under this app's config). Client side needs nothing: the PR #15 code already uses UDP streams when INFO offers them (tested by @0pcom against skywire's `wisp serve --direct`).

Things to decide: rate limits / abuse (open UDP relay to arbitrary hosts and ports), whether port 53 should stay on the relay's own resolver, and a reasonable per-connection stream cap.

title: Add native Android app framework
body:
Android users previously had no native client. This adds a Kotlin / Jetpack Compose foundation modeled on the iOS client, with an offline demo and a connection to the existing encrypted desktop remote-access service. Scientific computation stays on the desktop host.

## Changes

- Add `apps/android` with separate Compose `app` and pure JVM `remote` modules, a pinned Gradle wrapper, JDK 21 / SDK 36 configuration, and Android 8.0+ support.
- Implement the existing WSS / AES-GCM protocol, command capability checks, ordered requests, foreground reconnects, and current-connection snapshot gates. Uncertain mutations are not automatically replayed. Store credentials encrypted with Android Keystore.
- Add project and conversation navigation, text sending, one-time approvals, stopping, run logs, file text previews, monthly research history, and device-local text checklists / notebooks.
- Reuse the iOS synthetic demo assets and existing DTO contract fixtures. Export action icons from `compose_icon()` and reuse the existing app branding. Keep Back / Escape navigation in one window-level stack.
- Add Android CI plus setup, architecture, feature scope, and follow-up documentation in `apps/android/README.md` and `docs/development.md`.

## Validation

- 15 JVM protocol / demo / research tests passed, including Rust frame compatibility, tamper and direction checks, request ordering, reconnect without replay, project and path isolation, and calendar boundaries.
- 3 application state tests passed for stale snapshots, wrong routes, and uncertain operations.
- 5 instrumentation tests passed on Pixel9_API36 (Android 16, arm64), covering immediate Escape navigation, activity recreation, demo messages, offline notes, and encrypted credential persistence.
- Debug APK and instrumentation APK compiled; Android Lint passed with no errors. Existing tool-version and KTX style suggestions remain.
- Installed the final debug APK and visually checked the offline demo landing page. Diff whitespace checks passed.

## Manual smoke steps

1. Open `apps/android` in Android Studio, run `app`, and enter the bundled demo. Open a project, conversation, and files; Back or Escape should return exactly one level.
2. Send a demo message, inspect the preset reply, and approve or reject the sample request. Create a local checklist item or note, recreate the activity, and verify persistence.
3. With an owned online Wisp host, connect using its remote link and check sending, approvals, background / foreground recovery, and disconnects during an operation. This real-host validation has not been performed.

## Limitations and follow-up

This is the Android foundation, not full iOS feature parity. Follow up with rich Markdown and image rendering, uploads, older history, message queues, inbox / global calendar, disk read caching, checklist conflict sync, notebook sharing, and tablet multi-column layouts. Apple-specific OCR / camera processing is deferred behind an explicitly unavailable text-recognition interface. Local research notes do not sync yet. Release signing and store distribution are outside this PR.

title: fix(voice): コンテナにも VC の env を渡し、EC2 の反映手順を書く
body:
## 何が起きていたか

本番（Cloudflare Containers 経路）で `GET /api/v1/voice/token` が **503 `voice_unavailable`** を返し、VC が使えませんでした（実ブラウザで確認）。

- `frontend/worker/backend.ts` の `container.start({env})` に VC の環境変数を渡していなかった（`wispEnv` は渡していた）
- `frontend/cloudflare.config.ts` の `backendWorker.env` にもバインディングが無かった
- **Worker の env はコンテナへ自動で渡らない**。`cf containers applications edit --body` でも入れられない（DO 管理のコンテナは `observability.logs.enabled` しか変更できず、env は scheduler-backed のみ）

## 変更

- `frontend/cloudflare.config.ts`: `IUBEO_VC_PRIVATE_KEY`（secret）/ `IUBEO_VC_SIGNALING_URL` / `IUBEO_VC_MEDIA_URL`（text）を宣言
- `frontend/worker/backend.ts`: `voiceEnv` を追加し、**3 つ揃っているときだけ** `container.start` の env へ載せる（鍵が無い環境では今までどおり 503 で安全側）。署名だけなので `enableInternet: false` のまま
- `docs/voice-chat.md` / `.github/workflows/README.md`: 鍵の投入手順（`cf workers secrets update IUBEO_VC_PRIVATE_KEY --worker iubeo-backend --type secret_text --text <d>`）
- `infra/aws/terraform/README.md`: EC2 は `/etc/iubeo/env` を**初回起動時にしか作らない**ため、VC を入れる前に作ったインスタンスには入っていない（`deploy_command` でも入らない）。`terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.backend` か SSM で 3 行追記する手順を明記

## 検証

### Cloudflare Containers 経路（本番で稼働中）

- `pnpm typecheck` / `pnpm lint` / `pnpm test`（91 files / 900 tests）/ `cf build`
- **デプロイ済み**（secret 投入 → `cf deploy --mode backend`）
  - `GET /api/v1/voice/token`（セッション外）: 503 `voice_unavailable` → **403 `not_in_session`**
- 実ブラウザ（Chrome）でマッチング → セッション入りを確認
  - セッション中の `GET /api/v1/voice/token`: **200**（`room: sess-...` / signaling / mediaUrl / JWT）
  - `wss://vc.thirdlf03.com/v1/signaling` に接続
  - MoQ（WebTransport）の `start()` 成功 → `status: "ready"`、照準の輪が灰色（ready/待機）になる

> 音声そのもの（Opus の送受信）は相手が必要で、CPU は VC に入らないため未確認です。

### EC2 経路（実機に反映済み・現在は停止）

10/09 作成のインスタンスは VC コミット（10/11）より前で、動いていたイメージも `release-608d1b9` でした。実機で次を実施しました。

1. 起動 → `/etc/iubeo/env` に `IUBEO_VC_*` の 3 行を追記（`/etc/iubeo/env.bak-1791705008` にバックアップ）
2. `/usr/local/bin/iubeo-deploy` でイメージを `release-ae62ea98…`（VC 入り）へ更新
3. 確認: `docker inspect iubeo` の env に `IUBEO_VC_*` が入る / `curl localhost:8080/api/v1/voice/token` が **403 `not_in_session`**（503 ではない）/ `/healthz` OK / `iubeo-wisp` も起動
4. 停止して元の状態に戻した（転送先 `target` は `ec2` ではないので本番はコンテナのまま）

次に `/ec2start` で EC2 へ切り替えても VC は動きます。なお SSM のコマンド履歴に鍵が残ります（SSM に削除 API が無く 30 日で消える。`terraform.tfvars` / state と同じ露出なので、気になるなら鍵のローテーションを）。

## まだやっていないこと

- **Web Search タスクが Google の CAPTCHA に阻まれる件**（既定の検索先が `google.com/search` で、WISP の出口 IP がブロックされる）。別 PR で対応

title: feat(voice): セッション中の VC を MoQ で繋ぐ
body:
## 概要

セッション中の VC を、**デプロイ済みの `vc.thirdlf03.com` / `media.thirdlf03.com:4443` をそのまま使って**動くようにしました。ゲームのバックエンドがセッションに紐づいたトークンを発行するので、セッションの外からは入れません。

（draft）

## 構成

```
browser ──GET /api/v1/voice/token──▶ ゲームの backend（EC2）
   │                                   セッション参加者に EdDSA JWT を発行
   ├──wss──▶ vc-elixir  /v1/signaling    roster
   └──QUIC──▶ moq-relay  :4443           音声（Opus / datagram）
                 └─ /v1/moq/auth ──▶ vc-elixir  room の中だけ publish/subscribe
```

- トークンは VC サービスと同じ Ed25519 鍵で署名（`IUBEO_VC_PRIVATE_KEY` = VC ホストの `/etc/vc/keys/private.jwk` の `d`）
- `room` = セッション id、`sub` = プレイヤー id。moq-relay は `vc-bench/<room>/<sub>` の publish と `vc-bench/<room>/*` の subscribe だけを許す
- 位置はゲームの `transforms`（サーバーの正）を使い、VC 層は位置を知らない

## 変更
- `backend/internal/voice` … Ed25519(EdDSA) JWT の発行（vc の `docs/protocol.md` §1 と同じ形）
- `backend/internal/server/voice.go` … `GET /api/v1/voice/token`（セッション参加者のみ。居なければ 403）
- `frontend/src/voice/`
  - `store.ts` … トークン取得 → signaling → MoQ。状態は `useVoiceState`
  - `signaling.ts` / `moq.ts`（`@moq/net` 0.4.1 に固定）/ `audio.ts`（マイク AudioWorklet + 相手ごとの `PannerNode`）
  - `VoiceChat.tsx` … サンドボックスのセッション中だけマウント。毎フレーム、カメラを聞き手にする
- 操作は **HUD を足さず**、`V` push-to-talk / `M` ミュート。状態は**照準の細い輪**だけ（緑=送信、赤=ミュート、灰=待機）。開始直後だけ数秒ヒント
- terraform: `vc_private_key` / `vc_signaling_url` / `vc_media_url` を `/etc/iubeo/env` へ
- ドキュメント: `docs/voice-chat.md`

## 音質
- Opus **モノラル 48kbps / 20ms フレーム**（`latencyMode: realtime`）。`MoqVoice` の `bitrate` / `frameDurationMs` / `complexity` で調整可
- 実測 **45.4kbps**（32kbps から +40%）。WebCodecs は `opus` 拡張（frameDuration/complexity）に対応していることを確認済み
- Opus in-band FEC は**エンコードはできるが、WebCodecs の `AudioDecoder` に損失フレームを復元する API が無い**ため使っていない（理由を docs に記載）

## 確認したこと（実機）
- 発行した JWT が**デプロイ済み `vc-elixir` の `/v1/signaling` に通る**
- **MoQ が正しいこと**
  - ネゴシエートされたバージョン **`moq-lite-06`**（リレーの pin と一致）
  - 同室の2クライアントが相互に publish/subscribe（recv 470 フレーム / 38KB、errors 0）
  - **ルーム分離**: 別 room のクライアントは 486 フレーム送っても **recv 0**（漏れなし）
- **実際の音声**（2ブラウザ、A が `V` を6秒押して送信 → B が受信）

  - 送信元 RMS -20.5dB → 受信 -23.8dB（**損失 -3.3dB**）

- `go test ./...` / `go vet` / `gofmt` / `pnpm typecheck` / `pnpm lint` / `terraform validate`

title: Pollinations PR Submission — Quest #15923
body:
# Pollinations PR Submission — Quest #15923

## PR Title

**Add `apps/pi-browser`: the real Pi coding agent running in the browser, spending your own Pollen**

Fixes #15923

## PR Description

This adds **Pi in the Browser** under `apps/pi-browser` — the **real Pi coding agent** (the unmodified `pi` CLI v0.87.1 by earendil-works, loaded from the Wasmer registry as `wasmer/pi@=0.87.1`) running **entirely client-side** in a WebAssembly sandbox. There is no Pi-inspired reimplementation and no remote agent — the actual Pi binary executes in the page via the Wasmer SDK (WASIX + Web Workers), and every model call is paid with the visitor's own Pollen through **Bring Your Own Pollen**.

### What was used

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Pi agent** | `wasmer/pi@=0.87.1` from the Wasmer registry — the real Pi CLI running on Edge.js inside WASIX, with its bundled bash, coreutils, fd, ripgrep, grep, sed, findutils |
| **Wasmer SDK** | `@wasmer/sdk` 0.19.0 (`@wasmer/sdk/browser`) — sandbox creation, package loading with progress, filesystem access, process spawning. Vendored at install time (postinstall) so the SDK's worker/wasm URL resolution is untouched by bundlers |
| **BYO Pollen** | OAuth authorization-code flow **with PKCE** from `BRING_YOUR_OWN_POLLEN.md` — the user authorizes the app at `enter.pollinations.ai`, the app exchanges the code browser-side (PKCE, no secret), and the returned `sk_...` key is kept in memory/`sessionStorage` only |
| **Models** | `GET gen.pollinations.ai/v1` → tool-calling models fetched live; the chosen model is injected into the sandbox's `models.json` as an `openai-completions` provider with `baseUrl: https://gen.pollinations.ai/v1` — Pi speaks to Pollinations exactly like any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Switching models mid-session rewrites `models.json` live |
| **Network** | Browsers can't open TCP sockets, so Pi's HTTPS traffic is tunneled through a **WISP** server the visitor controls: one-click deploy of `wasmer/wisp-server` to a free Wasmer account (auto-configures the tab), a local `wasmer run wasmer/wisp-server --net`, or any `wss://` endpoint |
| **Automation** | Each message runs `pi --mode json --offline --provider pollinations --model <id> --tools read,write,edit,bash,grep,find,ls --session-id <id> "<prompt>"`; the app consumes Pi's JSONL event stream (streaming text, thinking, tool calls) and renders it live. Conversation continuity via Pi sessions inside the sandbox |

### How the app flow works

1. **Connect** — visitor clicks *Connect Pollinations account* → PKCE OAuth → their key + Pollen balance shown (they choose their own budget on the consent screen). An `sk_...` key can also be pasted directly.
2. **Pick a model** — live list of tool-calling Pollinations models with context size and Pollen pricing per million tokens.
3. **Network tunnel (WISP)** — one-click Wasmer deploy / local CLI / custom `wss://` URL. Can also be deferred; the app asks the first time Pi needs the network.
4. **Launch** — the app downloads `wasmer/pi@=0.87.1` (cached in browser storage afterwards) and boots a WASIX sandbox with an in-memory workspace seeded with a small starter project, plus `.pi/models.json`, `.pi/auth.json`, and an `APPEND_SYSTEM.md` that tells Pi about its browser environment.
5. **Work** — the visitor prompts Pi in a chat panel; Pi's text streams token-by-token, tool calls appear as live cards (bash command + output, file writes/edits), and the **workspace file tree updates live** with a built-in file viewer. Users can switch models, cancel runs, start fresh conversations, or restart the sandbox.

### Show one real end-to-end run

**Verified end-to-end run (recorded during development):**

Prompt: *"List the workspace, then write a marker file called e2e-result.txt."*

Pi executed, in the browser sandbox:
1. `bash: ls -la /workspace` — listed the seeded workspace
2. `write: e2e-result.txt` — created the file (appears live in the file tree; content verified in the file viewer)
3. Streamed the final answer describing what it did

The run was driven through the exact production path: app → sandbox → real `pi` v0.87.1 → `models.json` Pollinations provider → WISP tunnel → OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` → SSE stream → JSONL events → UI. For zero-spend verification the repo ships `mini-services/pi-e2e-fixture` (a scripted OpenAI-compatible endpoint + WISP server modelled on the Wasmer SDK's own Pi test fixture) — the same loop runs with any real Pollinations model once a key is connected. Screenshots: see `docs/` in the app folder (landing, workspace, agent run with tool cards, file viewer).

### How to run

```bash
cd apps/pi-browser
npm install        # postinstall vendors the Wasmer SDK into public/vendor
npm run dev        # http://localhost:3000 — needs COOP/COEP headers (next.config.ts sets them)
```

Create a publishable App Key at https://enter.pollinations.ai/keys with redirect URI `http://localhost:3000/` and set `NEXT_PUBLIC_POLLINATIONS_APP_KEY=pk_...` (or paste an `sk_...` key in the UI). Full details + browser limitations are in `apps/pi-browser/README.md`.

### Current browser limitations (also in the README)

- Requires cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers — included in `next.config.ts`)
- The sandbox filesystem is in-memory: files and Pi sessions reset on reload (packages are cached)
- Outbound networking needs the user-provided WISP tunnel
- No `git` inside the sandbox; long-running servers are discouraged (Pi is told via `APPEND_SYSTEM.md`)
- One `pi --mode json` process per message (~1–2 s startup each); conversation persists via Pi sessions

### Quest checklist

- [x] Live demo: ask Pi to create/edit a small project, run a command, see files and output
- [x] Runs Pi itself in the browser (real `pi` v0.87.1 via `wasmer/pi`), not a Pi-inspired agent or a remote UI
- [x] Visitor connects their Pollinations account, chooses a model, uses their own Pollen (BYOP)
- [x] App source under `apps/` + README with run instructions and browser limitations
- [x] Real end-to-end run shown (documented above + reproducible fixture)
- [x] Kept easy to understand: single-page app, ~6 focused source modules

title: Open the desktop Wisp from a browser through a self-hosted relay (#1460)
body:
Part of #1460 (phases 2–3: tunnel, pairing, a narrow-screen web page that can read, send, stop and approve).

## What it does

Deploy `wisp-relay` on any server. On the desktop, **Settings → Remote Access → Remote web access**: enter the relay URL and its `WISP_RELAY_TOKEN`, enable it, and Wisp shows a connection code (联机码) and a link `https://relay.example.com/remote#<code>`. Open the link on a phone, or open `/remote` and type the code. One relay serves any number of computers: each code derives its own rendezvous id, so different codes reach different machines.

```
browser ──HTTPS/WSS──> wisp-relay (ciphertext only) <──outbound WSS── desktop Wisp
```

The page lists projects → conversations → the latest transcript with tool calls and pending approvals showing the full command or diff. You can create a conversation, send, stop, approve or reject. It polls the snapshot every 1.5 s while a turn runs, 4 s otherwise, reconnects automatically, keeps unsent text on failure and never retries a mutation.

## Security

- **The relay never sees the code.** It lives in the URL fragment (never sent to servers). The relay sees only `sid = SHA-256("wisp-remote/sid/v1" ‖ code)[..16]`; frames are AES-256-GCM with `SHA-256("wisp-remote/key/v1" ‖ code)`. 128-bit code, kept in the OS keyring.
- **No reflection, replay or reordering.** AAD binds each frame's direction; every request carries the host's per-connection hello nonce and a strictly increasing sequence.
- **Only the relay token holder can register a computer.**
- **Small allowlist:** list projects/conversations, snapshot, create, send, stop, approve. Not exposed: terminal input, kernel execution, file save/actions, attachments, queued follow-ups, ACP conversations, and permanent approval scopes (approvals apply once).
- **Remote turns always ask.** The broker is stamped `remote` by the connection (never from the request) and remote sends run with the IM origin, so writes, edits and shell need approval even if the desktop default is Allow. Approval prompts are not mirrored to IM: those only go to per-frame progress observers, which remote turns don't register.
- The loopback native broker still rejects browser `Origin`s; the page never talks to the computer directly. The page uses `textContent` only, under `script-src 'self'` with no inline script.

## Implementation

| | |
|---|---|
| `crates/wisp-sync/src/remote.rs` | Rendezvous (`/v1/remote/host/{sid}` behind the relay token, `/v1/remote/client/{sid}`), code derivation, frame sealing, `/remote` + `/remote.js` |
| `crates/wisp-sync/src/remote.{html,js}` | Vanilla JS client, light/dark, phone-first |
| `src-tauri/src/channels/remote.rs` | Outbound tunnel with backoff and heartbeat, allowlist, `set_remote_access` / `reset_remote_access_code` |
| `native_settings.rs` | Broker is now shared (`broker(app)`), so it exists in normal desktop mode too; `context_label` extracted from `invoke_command` |
| `native_conversations.rs` | `remote_turn`: remote sends go through `send_message_inner` with `TurnOrigin::Im` |
| `ui/src/channels_view.rs` | New row + detail page next to Feishu / WeChat / StickS3 |
| `docs/remote-access.md` | Deployment (Caddy/nginx WebSocket config), security model, protocol |

The relay's WebSocket upgrade runs on the `tokio-tungstenite 0.30` the desktop already links, instead of axum's `ws` feature, which would pull in a second tungstenite.

## Not in this PR (still tracked in #1460)

Chunked attachment upload, command-result lookup after a dropped reply, actor columns in the store, per-connection delivery tiers, push, guest roles, proxy support for the desktop's outbound connection, and a real hostname on macOS (it shows `Wisp`).

## Testing

- `cargo test -p wisp-sync`: a fixed WebCrypto vector generated with Node's `crypto.subtle` must open in Rust (pins browser/Rust compatibility), plus a real WebSocket test: browser before host gets 4404, a host without the token is rejected, frames route both ways by connection id, and the host leaving closes its browsers.
- `cargo test -p wisp-tauri`: allowlist rejects the four RCE-equivalent commands, enqueue, attach and non-once approval scopes; requests replayed, reordered, from another connection, reflected or forged are dropped; `ChannelsStatus.remote` DTO contract.
- `cargo test --workspace`: 2669 passed, 0 failed.
- `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (ui), `cargo fmt --all -- --check`.
- Playwright: new `remote web access needs a relay…` spec plus the existing Remote Access/StickS3 specs (4/4).
- Manual browser smoke at 390×844: real `wisp-relay` + a scripted host speaking the tunnel protocol. Projects, conversations, transcript and approval render; Approve and Send round-trip; killing the host shows 电脑离线 and restarting it reconnects with a fresh nonce; no console errors.
- Not done: an end-to-end run with the real desktop app against a deployed relay.

title: Switch projects and conversations and preview files in remote web access (#1460)
body:
Part of #1460. Follows #1471.

## Problem

The remote page was a single column: projects → conversations → a plain-text transcript. Switching conversation meant backing out through two lists, the browser's Back button left the page, replies showed raw Markdown, pictures did not show at all, and there was no way to look at a file the agent had just written.

## What it does

The page now follows the desktop layout, for the moments you are away from the computer. It is deliberately not a full client.

- **Projects and conversations.** The project's conversations sit on the left under a project picker, the conversation in the middle. Rows show *Running* / *Needs you*; opening a finished conversation clears its *Needs you* flag on the desktop too. A phone shows one pane at a time and the back arrow steps out of it.
- **The address is the route.** `#<code>/p/<project>/s/<conversation>/f/<file>`: Back, reload and bookmarks work. Everything stays in the fragment, so the relay still learns neither the code nor what is open.
- **Replies.** Rendered as Markdown (headings, nested lists, tables, code, links) with their pictures inline. A file link in a reply opens that file's preview.
- **Files.** The folder button opens the conversation's project folder beside it. Text opens as text; Markdown is rendered; PDF and Office documents show the text the desktop already extracts from them; images open as pictures. An open folder refreshes every 8 s.

## Security

- **Allowlist adds four read-side commands**: directory listing, text preview, the bounded image thumbnail, and mark-as-seen. Upload, download, export, file actions, delete and the locations list stay rejected.
- **File reads are local and text only.** A non-local `context_id`, `render_pdf` or `render_office` is refused, and `base64` is dropped from the preview before the reply is sealed. Pictures only travel as the existing ≤1024 px re-encoded thumbnail, so no original file bytes leave the computer and nothing can be downloaded.
- **Nothing to sanitize.** The Markdown renderer builds a fixed set of elements from text nodes. HTML in a reply or a file is shown as text; links are limited to `http(s)`/`mailto` or an in-page file route; remote image URLs are never fetched. The CSP is unchanged.
- **One oversized reply no longer drops the tunnel.** The relay closes the host socket on a frame over 16 MiB, which disconnected every browser. Such a reply now fails that one request with an error.

This does not widen who can read what: a link holder could already ask the agent to read any project file.

## Relay container image

Deploying the relay on a server meant installing Rust there. The second commit packages it and publishes it.

- **Image.** `crates/wisp-sync/Dockerfile` builds only the relay: a static musl binary on an empty base, about 2 MB, running as uid 10001 with its data in a `/data` volume. Its ignore file sends just the manifests cargo needs.
- **Publishing.** The new `Relay Image` workflow builds amd64 and arm64 on their own runners (the same `ubuntu-24.04` / `ubuntu-24.04-arm` pair the Linux release uses) and publishes `ghcr.io/xuzhougeng/wisp-relay`: a release tag as `X.Y.Z` and `latest`, relay changes on main as `main`. Pull requests only build.
- **Docs.** Pulling or building the image, a compose file with Caddy for HTTPS, and running behind an existing proxy.

After the first publish, check the package visibility on GitHub: a new GHCR package can start private, in which case it needs to be set to Public once before servers can pull it without logging in.

## Changed files

| | |
|---|---|
| `crates/wisp-sync/src/remote.{html,js}` | Three-pane layout, fragment routing, Markdown renderer, image loading with a small cache, files pane. No new dependencies or relay routes. |
| `src-tauri/src/channels/remote.rs` | Allowlist additions and their argument checks, `strip_file_bytes`, `seal_reply` size guard. |
| `ui-tests/tests/remote-web.spec.ts` | New: the real page under the relay's CSP, against a fake host speaking the sealed-frame protocol over Playwright's WebSocket routing. No relay binary, desktop or network. |
| `docs/remote-access.md` | How to use the page, the file boundaries, what is intentionally left to the desktop, and running the relay in Docker. |
| `crates/wisp-sync/Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.dockerignore` | The relay image. |
| `.github/workflows/relay-image.yml` | Builds both architectures; publishes to GHCR outside pull requests. |
| `AGENTS.md`, `docs/project-sync*.md` | The release steps name the new tag-triggered workflow; project sync links to the Docker section. |

No changes under `ui/`, to the relay's Rust code, or to the wire protocol.

## Testing

- `cargo test -p wisp-tauri channels::remote` (4): the allowlist rejects upload/download/export/locations/delete and non-local or rendered file reads; previews keep text and drop file bytes (checked against the `native-files` contract fixture); an oversized reply becomes a per-request error; the existing replay/reorder test.
- `npx playwright test tests/remote-web.spec.ts` (5): project and conversation switching with Back and reload; Markdown and conversation images with raw HTML kept as text; folder browsing with text, truncated, Markdown, extracted-document, image and no-preview files; one-pane phone layout that keeps the conversation's scroll position under the files pane; missing or malformed codes. Each test also asserts no console errors under the CSP.
- `cargo test --workspace` and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` pass.
- Manual: the real `wisp-relay` binary with a scripted host and a real browser. Offline notice, automatic reconnect once the host registers, Markdown, image, file preview, a 9 MB text reply in one host frame, and the notice when the host goes away.

- Container, locally: the image builds and runs as uid 10001 on a fresh volume; the page and CSP are served; a write without the token is 401 and with it 204; data survives a restart; a host without the token is rejected; frames pass both ways, also through Caddy over HTTPS/WSS including a 9 MB frame; `docker stop` returns in half a second.
- The `Relay Image` workflow builds both architectures on this pull request.

Not done:

- The publish half of the workflow (login, push by digest, tagging). It cannot run before the workflow is on main; it follows Docker's documented multi-runner pattern.
- Certificate issuance for a real domain. The Caddy check used its internal certificate for `localhost`.

- An end-to-end run with the real desktop app. The desktop side is covered by unit tests and by the page being driven with payloads shaped like the shared DTOs.
- The full Playwright suite locally; only the new spec was run.

## Manual smoke

1. Run `wisp-relay`, enable **Settings → Remote Access → Remote web access**, open the link.
2. Pick a project, open a conversation, switch to another from the list, change project with the picker, then use the browser's Back.
3. Open a conversation whose reply contains a table and a figure; both should render.
4. Press the folder button, open a folder, a `.txt`, a `.md`, a `.png` and a PDF; a binary file should say it cannot be previewed.
5. Repeat 2–4 at phone width.

## Known limitations

Left to the desktop on purpose: rendered PDF/Office previews, downloads, uploads, earlier transcript pages, search, model and plan-mode controls, run cards, the terminal and notebooks. Files on remote execution contexts are not reachable. The page still polls (1.5 s while a turn runs, 4 s otherwise); there is no push. The remaining #1460 items are unchanged.

title: docs(apps): self-hosting names the apps runner headers; macOS apps gate in releasing
body:
## What

- **docs/WEB.md**, new "Apps on your own server" under Run it: from 1.2, a web server other than the Docker image needs `/app-frame.html` and `/app-frame-net.html` served with the runner policies from `apps/web/nginx.conf`.
  - The client asks `/app-frame.html` once for its header and hides Apps when it is missing or looser in the directives it checks (`apps/ui/src/lib/apps/runnerCheck.ts`). It does not check every directive, so the doc says to copy the whole value.
  - `/app-frame-net.html` is asked only when an app granted the internet opens (`webOpener.ts`), so the doc gives a `curl -sI` check for it too (`connect-src https: wss:`).
  - Every other path keeps the site's policy (`apps/web/nginx-headers.conf`, `frame-src 'self'`); a site policy that blocks frames breaks every app although Apps shows.
  - `npm run dev -w @ghostly/web` and `npm run preview -w @ghostly/web` send both headers (the root `npm run dev` serves `apps/ui`, which does not).
- **docs/INSTALLATION.md**: the Self-hosted line points there.
- **docs/RELEASING.md**, a new step 3 before Publish: a manual check of apps on the macOS Desktop app before publishing a release with Apps on. `e2e/desktop/apps.spec.ts` runs on Linux only and `e2e/desktop-macos/` has no apps spec. Steps: install Chess from the default store, open it in a 1:1 chat (a window of its own, which is what shows it was hardened: on macOS a window without its rule list or WebKit configuration never opens), play and reopen. A `WebKit has no feature <key>` log line does not block the release by itself: it is written down and checked against the required layers of WISP 1200.
- Changelog fragment `apps-self-hosting-docs.md` with `release: 1.2`. The key takes effect once #1482 (changelog release holds) lands; until then `changes.mjs` and `bump-version.mjs` ignore it.

Docs only. `APPS_ENABLED` stays false.

## Tests

- `node tools/scripts/changes.mjs`: 17 fragments, all well formed.
- `vitest run -c tools/scripts/vitest.config.ts readme changes` (2 workers): 22 passed.
