title: Fixing ReferenceError in selenite proxy on Netlify site
body:
🔗 **View agent run:** https://app.netlify.com/projects/segleg/agent-runs/6ac6ccfa6d4c851ffd9c82b9

🤖 **Agent:** Claude

💬 **Prompt:** i made a selenite proxy on my netlify website, the website opens but when i type in an url, this happens: ReferenceError: __uv$config is not defined the url i typed in was https://youtube.com

✅ **Result:** Submitting a URL on the deployed Selenite proxy failed with `ReferenceError: __uv$config is not defined`. The cause was the site's 404 page. Before the Ultraviolet service worker takes over the `/purple/service/...` route, Netlify serves `404.html` for that path, and that page tried to load Ultraviolet from a `woah/` folder that doesn't exist. It also used relative script paths, which point to the wrong place when the page is served from a nested URL. Because Ultraviolet's config never loaded, the service worker registration crashed.

The 404 page now loads the real Ultraviolet, bare-mux and Epoxy files from absolute paths. It also loads the error/"register serviceworker" script that was missing, and no longer references scripts that don't exist or that belong only to the home page. The home page's scripts and styles also use absolute paths now, so they load correctly from any URL.

There is still one limitation: Netlify only hosts static files and can't run the Wisp WebSocket server that Ultraviolet uses to fetch websites. With this fix the `__uv$config` error is gone, but pages like YouTube still won't load until the proxy points to a Wisp server hosted somewhere else, such as a VPS, Railway or Koyeb. To make that easier, `public/register-sw.js` now has a `wispServer` setting at the top. Set it to your server's address (for example `wss://your-wisp-server.example.com/wisp/`). If you leave it empty, the proxy uses `/wisp/` on the current host, which keeps working when you run the full app with `npm start`.

title: feat(apps): Desktop opens an installed app in an app window of its own (marketplace PR 11)
body:
Marketplace PR 11 (WISP 1200, Desktop row): an installed app opens on Desktop in an `app-*` window of its own instead of a frame. Behind the apps flag.

**How it works**
- The web broker (`createBroker`) runs in the Ghostly window, one instance per app window (`apps/ui/src/lib/apps/desktopOpener.ts`, registered with `setAppOpener` in `apps/ui/src/main.tsx`). The API and its caps are the web's: `context`, `file`, `storage.*`, `chat.send/on`, `close`, 64 KiB, 50 a second.
- Rust's `app_broker` is now async. It answers the runner's `start` itself (the entry, once, and "Not ready" until the Linux filter is in). It checks the label, 64 KiB and 50/s on its own too, then hands every other request to the Ghostly window with the caller's label and returns the answer as its result. Events go back by `webview.eval("window.__ghostlyEvent(<serde_json>)")` on that label only.
- New commands, callable from the Ghostly window only: `app_open` (async, off the main thread), `app_post`, `app_close`. A window the person closes stops its broker there (`ghostly-app-closed`), so the chat's app closes on the contact's side.
- The runner choice comes from the engine's grant. An app with `internet` gets the network runner's CSP and a second rule list (macOS) or filter (Linux) that lets only `https:` and `wss:` through. WebRTC stays off and navigation stays locked (`about:srcdoc` and `about:blank` refused).
- Desktop serves its runner itself (`appRunnerServed`), so Apps does not fetch a header there.
- Windows: `app_open` refuses with "Apps do not run on Windows yet…". WebView2's equivalents are not measured; recorded in the WISP.
- `__TAURI_INTERNALS__` stays in app pages. Tauri defines it as non-configurable and answers every call through `window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__.runCallback`. Recorded as a residual in the threats row, with the gates that hold (coordinator OK).

**Measured on macOS 15.6 (WKWebView)** with `apps/desktop/fixtures/app-sandbox/measure.mjs`, guards `full` and `internet`:
- full: 0 hits on any listener (fetch, img, ws, wss, https, preconnect, STUN/TURN). Frames refused (`about:blank`, `about:srcdoc`). 109 other commands refused, `too-large` over 64 KiB, `too-fast` in a burst of 60. `delete __TAURI_INTERNALS__` leaves it in place.
- internet: only TLS connections (https fetch, https image, wss), 7 hits. No plain HTTP, no preconnect, no WebRTC, the same refusals.

**Tests**
- Rust: label identity (a forged app/window is still the caller), only_main both ways for the 4 commands, 64 KiB, id and type checks, the 50/s window, answers reaching only their own window, events as JSON, both CSPs, both rule lists, the Linux wait. `cargo test --lib`: 259 pass. clippy is clean.
- UI: `desktopOpener.test.ts` (10), `appsTestFetch.test.ts`, the runnerServed case in `appsUi.test.tsx`, the desktop net CSP in `contentSecurityPolicy.test.ts`.
- Linux Desktop e2e `e2e/desktop/apps.spec.ts`: it installs Chess from a test store served locally, opens it, switches WebDriver to the app-* window and checks the API, the caps and the refusals there, then the app closes itself. `e2e.yml`'s Desktop build gets `VITE_APPS_TEST=1`. Run: see the comment below.

title: feat(apps): the web runner and broker for mini-apps, behind the apps flag (marketplace PR 6)
body:
Ghostly 1.2 marketplace, PR 6: the web runner and broker (WISP 1200, "The runner and the broker"), plus the owner's 2026-10-06 decisions: the `internet` permission, and Safari not restricted, with the preconnect residual documented. This is a draft for the coordinator's review; nothing merges before that.

Everything is behind `APPS_ENABLED`. There is no user-visible entry point (PR 7 adds the Apps page and the card).

## What it adds
**Two runners, one file: `apps/web/public/app-frame.html`.**
- The runner deletes `RTC*` and refuses unless its origin is "null" and it has a parent.
- It nonce-locks the page and checks the lock with a probe frame.
- It takes one port from the parent only, says `writing`, waits for the ack, then writes the entry. Every script is built before the first one goes in, and after that the runner calls only functions it captured at its start.
- `/app-frame.html` serves the runner CSP; `/app-frame-net.html` (the same file) serves the network CSP, for apps the person granted `internet`. The network CSP adds `https:`/`wss:` to connect, img, media and font. Script, frames, workers, forms and plain HTTP stay shut, and WebRTC is still deleted.

**Hint guard (defence in depth).** In WebKit `<link rel=preconnect>` connects under any policy.
- The runner strips `<link>`, `iframe`, `frame`, `object`, `embed` and speculation rules from the entry, declarative shadow roots included.
- It guards the DOM's ways in (`appendChild` and its kin, `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `setHTMLUnsafe`, `Range`), runs an observer, and withholds `document.write`.
- It sits in one marked block. An e2e build (`VITE_APPS_TEST`) also emits `/app-frame-unguarded.html`, so the nonce lock is measured on its own.

**Server and build.**
- nginx: a location per runner. Neither includes ghostly-headers.conf; the other headers are repeated, plus `X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off`. The main CSP gets `frame-src 'self'`.
- The Vite dev and preview servers send the same headers.
- All three runner paths are in the service worker's `NEVER`.

**Broker, `apps/ui/src/lib/apps/broker.ts`.**
- One port, exactly one `load` after `writing`.
- The WISP API: `context`, `file`, `storage.*` per app and chat, `chat.send`/`chat.on`, `close`. 64 KiB requests, 50 a second.
- Identity comes from the port. The runner is chosen from the granted permissions (`runnerFor`), never from the app.

**Platform.** `ServicesPlatform.apps` (`AppsPlatform`), `BrowserHost.appRunner`/`appNetRunner`, `engineApps()` on the #1360 and #1366 RPCs, `open.ts` for PR 7, a web opener, and a runner header check that hides Apps on a server without it.

**Core.** `internet` joins `APP_PERMISSIONS`, with a new valid vector (existing vectors unchanged). Adding it in an update asks again (`addedAppPermissions`, tested).

**Test flag.** `VITE_APPS_TEST=1` is build-time only and refused in image builds.

**WISP 1200.**
- The nonce lock and the app contract: no inline `on*` handlers, no scripts after start, no `<link>` or frames, no `document.write`.
- The `internet` permission (manifest, table, install line, the network runner's CSP, the Desktop rule-list note).
- The WebKit-web preconnect residual, and Safari's install line.
- Two change files.

## e2e/web/apps-sandbox.spec.ts, 10 tests (local; the page carries the production CSP)
| | Chromium 145 | WebKit 26 | Firefox 155 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tests | 10/10 | 10/10 | 10/10 |
| Control (no runner): probes reached | 50 | 54 | 48 |
| Runner (guard on), no `internet`: HTTP, HTTPS/WSS, 6 preconnect ways, 16 WebRTC frame ways | 0 | **0** | 0 |
| Nonce lock alone (no guard): WebRTC from 16 frame kinds | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Nonce lock alone: preconnect | 0 | 6/6 connect (expected, documented) | 0 |
| `internet` granted: HTTPS fetch, image, WSS | reach the listener | same | same |
| `internet` granted: plain HTTP, remote script, frame, form, WebRTC | refused | same | same |
| Nonce read by the app | no | no | no |
| Another app's storage via forged fields | refused | same | same |
| Flood / 64 KiB+ | too-fast / too-large | same | same |
| reload, document.open | torn down | torn down | torn down |
| Self-navigation, meta refresh, link, ping | torn down, 0 hits | torn down, 0 hits | refused before any load, 0 hits |

Also run: chat.spec and compat-chat (7/7) against the flagged build. A release build has no test hook and no unguarded runner.

Run it: `E2E_WEB_PORT=<port> npx playwright test -c e2e/playwright.config.ts --project=web e2e/web/apps-sandbox.spec.ts`, then `-c e2e/playwright.webkit.config.ts` and `-c e2e/playwright.firefox.config.ts`.

title: Update wisp to v0.8.0
body:
Bumps the pinned upstream release from v0.7.0 to v0.8.0 (commit 687faf8). wisp now requires Zig 0.17, so the build stage downloads 0.17.0 and checks it against the sha256s from ziglang.org for both architectures.

v0.8.0 has no protocol or configuration changes from 0.7.0; it picks up two upstream WebSocket fixes (a wss read that could leave a received message unread on a quiet connection, and a buffer resize that handed memory to the wrong allocator). No migration.

Built the x86_64 image from this Dockerfile and ran it: it starts as v0.8.0, NIP-11 reports `0.8.0`, it accepts an event, and an oversized `limit` gets EOSE.

title: Hide what a stranger can't use; help and docs without milestone numbers (#342, #343)
body:
A stranger who installs illogical, reads the README, runs `illogical --help` and adds the MCP server shouldn't meet Fountain, studio, chant workspaces, VM tabs or guest ssh. They belong to our own setup. They're hidden, not removed: each still works for anyone who knows the command.

Two commits:

**Hide what a stranger can't use (#342)**
- **CLI:**
  - Hidden commands: `fountain`, `studio`, `app`, `workspace`, `guests`, `machines`, `sandboxes`.
  - Hidden options: `agent`'s `--fountain`/`--as`/`--vault`/`--vm`; `run`'s `--vm`/`--vm-tab`/`--image`/`--sandbox`; `share`'s `--guest` and the options that go with it.
  - `illogicald`: `--studio-file`, the wisp, sandbox and VM-agent key flags, and the guest ssh flags.
  - `illogical <cmd> --help` still works for each.
- **MCP:**
  - `open_app`, `open_workspace`, `list_agents`, `read_agent` and `open_fountain` are left out of the tool list (`UNLISTED`). Dispatch still answers them by name.
  - The server instructions and the `run`, `send_input`, `close` and `start_agent` descriptions lose their Fountain, app and VM text. Schema parameters are unchanged.
- **Swarm:** only `blocks`, and no picker when there's one theme. city, hive and timeline stay in the code. A saved theme that isn't offered falls back to blocks.
- **Web:**
  - "Invite over ssh…" in a pane's menu is hidden.
  - Both that item and the other swarm themes come back with the browser key `illogical.more = "1"`, which is how their e2e specs reach them. That key is the only switch: real per-feature flags are #347, after launch.
- **Docs:** the README's Fountain runner section and the hidden tools in its MCP allowlist are gone. `docs/features.md`, `cli.md`, `advanced.md` and `teams.md` drop Fountain, studio, workspaces, VM tabs, guest ssh and the extra themes.

**Help and docs without milestone numbers or internal names (#343)**
- Every command's help starts with one short line, so `illogical --help` is a list of one-liners.
- M- and S-numbers and `(#N)` are gone from `illogical` and `illogicald` help, the README and `docs/{features,cli,advanced,teams,control}.md`. `geek` and `wss://geek…` became `home.example.ts.net`.
- The README opens with the site's pitch: keeping track of your agents without checking every session. The swarm and agent blocks come before "Mouse first".

**Tests**
- New, each guarding one of the above: hidden but there (CLI), no numbers or internal names and short summaries (CLI and daemon help), no milestone numbers (README and docs), unlisted tools aren't listed but answer, and the instructions leave out what's hidden. Plus `swarm-themes.spec.ts` for the picker.
- Tool counts in the existing tests updated (39 → 34 after main's invite and attach tools). The Fountain tests still call the hidden tools by name and pass.
- 16 mutations, all caught.

**Not in this PR:**
- `docs/control-e2e.md` and `docs/research.md` keep their design-note numbers.
- The MCP schemas' `vm`/`fountain_agent` parameter docs still mention VM and Fountain.
- Control's page still offers "New hosted VM".
- Huddles and chat are untouched, pending #242.

Closes #342
Closes #343

title: Revisão do navegador, etapa 2: o lado do motor (VSSH-288)
body:
A etapa 2 do [VSSH-288](https://huly.colabh.org/workbench/cpps/tracker/VSSH-288), a revisão da arquitetura do navegador embutido, do lado do motor. Cada commit corresponde a um card. O comentário de entrega de cada card no Huly diz o que mudou e qual bancada mede a mudança.

O par deste PR é [colabhd/vssh-sso#63](https://github.com/colabhd/vssh-sso/pull/63), com o lado do portal e do shell.

## O que muda

Backend e wisp
- Um caminho com escape malformado responde 400, sem derrubar o processo (VSSH-290).
- A régua de rede: o loopback só para a porta da própria conta, a rede privada só com o nível 2 ou mais que o portal manda em `X-Vssh-Rede-Nivel`, e o metadata da nuvem nunca. O wisp ganha freio, teto de streams e timeout (VSSH-293, VSSH-291).
- `GET /versao` junta os `BUILD.json` dos pacotes, responde 503 quando falta um essencial, e os bundles saem numa URL versionada e imutável (VSSH-297, VSSH-320).
- O manifesto declara `recursos.metricas`, e o backend conta conexões, streams, falhas de DNS e upgrades recusados (VSSH-319).

Scramjet e controller
- O commit `b14b709a` do upstream, que faz o rewriter reescrever o corpo de uma declaração exportada, mais `efc723bf` e `783030b4` (VSSH-292).
- Os PRs 187, 186 e 188 do upstream, ainda abertos lá, e o wrapper que não gruda na palavra-chave anterior. O runway deixa de esperar falha em 14 casos que passam (VSSH-294).
- A página de erro de navegação do controller é um documento marcado, que o shell lê (VSSH-304).
- O cache de páginas guarda com teto, sem ler a resposta inteira antes de devolvê-la (VSSH-300).
- O wasm do rewriter usa o base64 nativo do navegador nas duas pontas (VSSH-299).
- O motor diz ao shell se a página empilhou ou trocou a URL (VSSH-312).

Transporte e bibliotecas C
- A exceção de certificado vale para um host só (VSSH-311), também no `wss://` (VSSH-295).
- curl 8.22.0, do tarball de release com os dois patches rebaseados em `client/tools/patches/curl/`, e mbedtls 3.6.7. O release sai sem as asserções do emscripten, e o `lib/libcurl_full.mjs` vendorizado é desse build (VSSH-295).
- O `upstream.yml` desconta o que já foi trazido ou recusado, conta o enxerto inteiro e avisa das dependências fora de `engines/` (VSSH-296).

## Testes

- A suíte do backend fica em 46/46, com 1 pulado.
- `bench/portal/` contra o transporte reconstruído: `certificado-por-host` (com o caso `wss://` novo), `primeira-carga` (10/10 diretas), `cookies-dominio` e `cache-de-paginas` passam.

O que ficou sem medida aqui:
- `transporte-run`, `ab-run` e `suite-run` deram 0/40 no container da revisão também com o transporte anterior. A saída de rede dele reassina o TLS com uma CA própria, e a trust store do wasm a recusa. As três precisam rodar no CI ou numa máquina com saída direta.
- A página de erro do controller não tem bancada neste repositório. A ponta do shell que lê o documento está coberta no vssh-sso (`tests/browser/erro-da-aba.test.js`).

O `backend/vendor/` fica de fora do diff: o job `vendor` da entrega o remonta e o commita no main.

## Ordem do deploy

Publicar depois do deploy do colabhd/vssh-sso#63. Sem o cabeçalho `X-Vssh-Rede-Nivel`, este motor trata a conexão como nível 0 e recusa a rede privada, e quem manda o cabeçalho é o portal daquele PR. Antes de instalar a versão nova numa estação, vale conferir o nível dela em Conexão e rede, no painel.

Depois do merge, rodar o `upstream.yml` por `workflow_dispatch`, para a issue #5 cair para os commits que faltam.

title: Wisp session has no reconnect: dead socket retried every 60s (libcurl error 55), fresh 502 'websocket did not open'
body:
## Observed (LobsterBrowse beta, zeolite 3.0 Diamond engine, 2026-10-05)

Two related symptoms, both pointing at the wisp session lifecycle having no transparent reconnect:

### 1. Dead wisp socket retried forever with libcurl error 55

Client log (wikipedia load, page itself worked):

```
2026-10-05T14:22:37Z error load failed: zeolite: stream: TypeError: Request failed with error code 55: Failed sending data to the peer
... (repeats ~1/sec for 20s, then)
2026-10-05T14:23:52Z .. 15:07:52Z error load failed: zeolite: stream: TypeError: Request failed with error code 55: Failed sending data to the peer
```

After the initial burst the retry settles into exactly one attempt every 60 seconds (all at :52.7) for over 44 minutes on the same dead socket. Error 55 is libcurl CURLE_SEND_ERROR: the underlying wisp WebSocket is gone, but the session keeps handing the dead socket to new requests once per minute instead of detecting the close and re-establishing the wisp connection.

### 2. Fresh session 502s with "websocket did not open"

After a hard reload (post epoxy deploy, transport selector had been switched to epoxy), recurring fresh 502 error pages:

```
Category: stream
Reason: Error: Hyper client: hyper_util::client::legacy::Error(Connect, WebSocketConnectFailed("websocket did not open"))
(client error (Wisp WebSocket failed to connect: websocket did not open))
Status: 502
Engine: zeolite 3.0 Diamond
```

This is not a one-off restart race: it recurs across hard reloads. The browser WebSocket to wss://<origin>/wisp/ never opens (under epoxy transport the connection is made by the epoxy-tls wasm itself, wisp_v2: true). No fallback and no retry/backoff on the client side.

## Gap

Neither transport path implements reconnect:
- The wisp WebSocket lifecycle lives inside the vendored transport (libcurl / epoxy-tls), not in sw.ts JS, and nothing in the SW detects a dead wisp session and re-initializes the transport.
- A failed initial WS open surfaces as a terminal 502 with no retry.

## Suggested direction

- Surface transport lifecycle events (wisp socket open/closed/error) from the wasm boundary to the SW so the SW can tear down and re-create the transport/session.
- Exponential backoff reconnect on socket close.
- On WS open failure, retry before serving the 502 page.

## Repro hints

- Symptom 1: load a page, keep the tab open >60 min (or kill the network briefly), watch the once-per-minute error 55 line in the client log.
- Symptom 2: with transport selector on epoxy, hard reload and navigate; 502 "websocket did not open" page appears. Switching the selector back to libcurl was proposed as an isolation test (pending user confirmation).

Environment: LobsterBrowse beta/zeolite-nativetransit (epoxy vendored + /epoxy route deployed 2026-10-05), zeolite 3.0 Diamond, Render deploy.

title: Export Velora for S3 and remove the opening PNG from Cloudflare
body:
Export the actual Velora client and proxy runtime for HTTPS S3 hosting instead of embedding the Cloudflare desktop. `npm run export:s3` produces a ZIP containing local app pages, assets, the proxy service worker, and an upload helper with exact S3 route objects and correct MIME types. The S3 package keeps the opening PNG splash; normal Cloudflare builds omit the PNG and start Velora directly.

Static domain registration explains its Cloudflare server requirement. Missing Games/Pyrite assets are reported in the manifest and README.

Fourteen tests passed for the relay default/custom override and S3 packaging. title: Fix Netlify deploy error by updating pnpm lockfile
body:
🔗 **View agent run:** https://app.netlify.com/projects/tst35/agent-runs/6abea076c812b5974be9bbea

🤖 **Agent:** Claude

💬 **Prompt:** The Netlify deploy errored, with the following guidance provided:

The build is failing at [line 27-28](#L27-L28) because the `pnpm-lock.yaml` lockfile is out of sync with the current `patchedDependencies` configuration in `package.json`. Netlify run...

✅ **Result:** 
Once the site deployed, every action showed "something went wrong". Interstellar is built to run behind its own Express server (`src/server.js`), but on Netlify only the static files in `dist` are served, so two things stopped working.

First, the build gives the Apps, Games, Tabs and Settings pages random per-build URLs, and only the Express server knew how to map those URLs back to the page files. A small post-build step (`scripts/netlify-redirects.js`) now writes a Netlify `_redirects` file from the build's route map. It also serves `/play.html`, proxies the `/gh-games/` game asset mirrors to GitHub as the server used to, uses the custom 404 page, and keeps the internal `.runtime` build manifest from being served publicly.

Second, browsing through the proxy needs a Wisp WebSocket server, which the Express server normally provides at `/wisp/`. Netlify can't host long-lived WebSocket connections. The build now accepts an optional `WISP_URL` setting that becomes the site's default Wisp server. `netlify.toml` sets it to the public MercuryWorkshop instance (`wss://wisp.mercurywork.shop/`). A Wisp URL that a visitor enters on the Settings page still takes priority. Self-hosted deployments that don't set `WISP_URL` keep using their own `/wisp/` endpoint. Uptime and privacy of the public Wisp server are outside this site's control, and the server can be swapped by changing `WISP_URL`.

title: Production deployment, frontend redesign, and security fixes
body:
## Summary

This PR has three parts:
1. A production setup that puts Wisp online at `https://your-domain` with one command.
2. A redesign that replaces the generic pastel look with a design built for Wisp.
3. Fixes for every high and medium finding from a full security review.

### 1. Production deployment (`docker-compose.prod.yml`)
- **Stack:** the app, PostgreSQL, Redis, Caddy (automatic Let's Encrypt HTTPS, which browsers require for camera/mic), coturn (TURN relay so calls connect on mobile data; it refuses to relay into private networks), and a backup service that writes a compressed database dump every 24h.
- **`Dockerfile`:** multi-stage build. Migrations and the idempotent catalog seed run when the container starts. The healthcheck uses the new `/api/health`.
- **Server:** shuts down cleanly on SIGTERM. `deploy/restore.sh` restores a backup.
- **`docs/DEPLOY.md`:** step-by-step guide covering the server, DNS, firewall, admin account, backups and updates.
- **Fix:** in production, avatars uploaded while the app was running were never served, and the first upload on a fresh install failed. The server now serves `/uploads/*` itself (images only, protected against path traversal) and creates missing folders.

### 2. Frontend redesign
Built following the frontend-design skill: plan, review against generic defaults, build, critique from screenshots. The design rules are in `docs/DESIGN.md`.
- **Idea: "two lights".** Violet is always you and mint is always the other person: chat bubbles, online dots, the logo.
- **Type:** Bricolage Grotesque for condensed poster headlines. Atkinson Hyperlegible for body and chat text.
- **Landing page:** the headline sits next to a short chat that plays once. "How it works" is a real sequence, safety is plain facts, and the feature cards are gone.
- **App:** text/voice/video toggle and a radio list on Discover, and a "How old are you?" guest entry. The end-of-chat screen says what actually happened. Empty states point to a next step.
- **Fixes along the way:**
  - A global CSS rule overrode every border color.
  - The radius scale inflated most elements.
  - Small form text made iPhones zoom in on focus.
  - Some match-mode descriptions were inaccurate.

### 3. Security fixes
| Severity | Problem | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| High | A logged-in token kept working for its full 30 days after logout, password reset, account deletion, ban or demotion. Banned users could use every API, and demoted admins kept admin. | Every request checks the session row and reads role and status from the database. |
| High | The dev compose file exposed Postgres (`wisp` password) and Redis (no password) on all interfaces. | Bound to `127.0.0.1`. |
| Medium | Clients could spoof `X-Forwarded-For` to bypass every per-IP rate limit. | Honored only from loopback/private proxies, using the entry the proxy appended. |
| Medium | Open redirect via `/login?next=`. | Same-site paths only. |
| Medium | WebSocket frames up to 100 MB. Reactions relayed free text past the message filter. Client metadata was stored unchecked. | 64 KB cap, whitelisted kinds and reactions, metadata rebuilt server-side. Music links are http(s) only and now reach the other person. |
| Medium | Bans didn't close live chat connections, and timeouts were never enforced. | Redis pub/sub closes a user's sockets. Timeouts block chat and default to 24h. |
| Medium | Moderators could suspend admins, and anyone could act on themselves. | Staff can only act on lower roles. |
| Medium | One permanent TURN password was shared with every guest. | Per-user logins that expire after 12h (coturn `use-auth-secret`). |
| Medium | A weak or example `AUTH_SECRET` would let anyone sign admin sessions. | The server refuses to start with one. |
| Bug | Two logins in the same second produced identical tokens, and the second failed with a 500. | Unique `jti` per token. |

**Upgrade note:** production `.env` files now need `TURN_SECRET` (`openssl rand -hex 32`) instead of `TURN_USERNAME`/`TURN_PASSWORD`, and `AUTH_SECRET` must be at least 32 characters.

The low-severity findings (room signaling targets, re-joining after removal, enumeration timing, avatar body size, CSP inline scripts and others) are not in this PR.

## Test plan
- [x] `tsc`, `eslint` clean. 165/165 tests pass (up from 109) and `npm run build` passes.
- [x] Security fixes re-tested end to end against the same exploits:
  - An old cookie after logout gets 401.
  - A banned user gets 401 on every API.
  - A spoofed IP hits the rate limit on the 11th request.
  - A ban closes an open socket with 4003, and the user can't reconnect.
  - A moderator can't suspend an admin, and an admin can't ban themselves.
  - A timed-out user can't open chat.
  - A demoted moderator loses access immediately.
  - A login with `?next=https://evil.example` lands on `/discover`.
  - coturn accepts valid per-user logins and rejects expired or forged ones.
- [x] User-flow regression after the security changes:
  - Messages go both ways.
  - Reactions, music share (now with its link), connect and report all work.
  - Rooms work.
  - Logout works.
- [x] Full production stack run locally over HTTPS:
  - Guest login and `wss://` chat through Caddy work.
  - Avatars upload and are served.
  - Data survives restarts, and a backup restores.
- [x] Redesign reviewed from screenshots on phone and desktop in light and dark mode. No sideways scrolling at 360/768/1280px.
- [ ] Not run here: the `apt-get install openssl` step in the Dockerfile, because this sandbox blocks Debian's package mirror. I verified the image on `node:22-bookworm`, which already includes OpenSSL.

title: WebSocket traffic is not proxied through /r
body:
The engine rewrites HTTP(S) subresources but WebSocket connections made by proxied pages hit the target origin directly and fail (sandboxed iframe + wrong origin) or bypass the proxy entirely if allowed. Sites that depend on WS (live chat, collaborative docs, some dashboards) partially break.

Options:
- Proxy WS through the server: rewrite ws:// wss:// URLs to a /ws route that bridges to the target using tokio-tungstenite, keeping the cookie jar semantics.
- Or route page WebSockets through the existing wisp endpoint via the injected shim (rewrite window.WebSocket to speak the wisp protocol over the /wisp/ upgrade).

title: 2.3: worker fetch() root-relative URL base wrong; WebSocket bridge from proxied pages closes 1006
body:
Two findings from a Tier-6 workers/WebSocket probe run against the 2.3 Selenide dist bundle (embedded at an origin, SW active and controlling, Chromium module SW, stock wisp relay). Both reproduce deterministically with any fixture host.

## 1. Root-relative fetch inside virtualized workers resolves to the wrong path

A proxied page spawns a classic worker whose code does fetch("/data.json") and posts the body back. Result: the request goes through the engine transport to the right host but the wrong path - the target's 404 body comes back ("not found" from the fixture), i.e. the root-relative URL resolved as if the base were the page route (/prefix/<encoded-page>/) instead of the virtual origin root. Same for a module worker.

Control: a page-level fetch of the same URL through an explicitly encoded route returns the correct 200 body, so route encoding and transport are fine; the defect is the URL base inside the virtualized worker (both classic and module).

## 2. WebSocket from a proxied page closes 1006 without open/error

The same proxied page opens:
- a relative WebSocket: (location.protocol === "https:" ? "wss://" : "ws://") + location.host + "/ws"
- an absolute wss:// to the target host's /ws endpoint

Both close with code 1006; neither onopen nor onmessage ever fires (onerror, when it fires, is immediately followed by close 1006).

Control: from a normal (non-proxied) page on a different origin, new WebSocket("wss://<same target host>/ws") connects, echoes a frame, and closes cleanly (open, message, close 1000). The target runs a minimal RFC6455 echo on /ws. So the endpoint and cross-origin WS are fine; the failure is in the engine's WebSocket interception/bridge inside proxied pages (both the proxy-origin relative form and the absolute target form).

## Repro

Serve any host with:
- /worker.js: self.onmessage doing fetch("/data.json") and postMessage of the body
- /ws: RFC6455 echo
- a page with the two probes above

Load the page through the engine prefix in a controlled context and read the probe results. Engine error-page meta confirms version 2.3 Selenide.

title: shell: make the WISP transport pluggable (openWispTransport)
body:
`WispSlirp` uses exactly seven members of its socket — `binaryType`, `onopen`, `onmessage`, `onclose`, `onerror`, `send()` and `close()` — so it is already duck-typed; it just happened to construct the WebSocket inline. This makes that a choice. `openWispTransport(url)` returns a real WebSocket for `ws://` and `wss://`, so the default path is unchanged, and any other scheme can supply an adapter.

What we needed it for is a WISP backend running inside the page, which cannot be a WebSocket at all: a page cannot listen, and a service worker cannot intercept `ws://`. So `vnet:<port>` dials a virtual-loopback port in the page and length-prefixes each packet (uint32 little-endian, matching WISP's own multi-byte fields), since a byte stream has no message boundaries. With that, the guest's TCP rides a mesh backend instead of a hosted relay — your v1 client worked against it unmodified, no changes to `WispSlirp` itself.

The second commit defers the SYN-ACK on the WISP connect path by 10 ms, the way the `gateway:80` branch just above it already does. We hit a main-thread wedge injecting it from inside the guest's own TX callback on the first by-IP connect. That was with the in-page transport; we have not reproduced it on the WebSocket path, so please read it as a precaution rather than a fix for something you are hitting — happy to drop that commit if you would rather.

Based on a74368e, and not tested against the newer build deployed at next.linuxontab.com — see #4.

title: feature/linux-kernel-integration: fresh clone doesn't boot — committed shell/linux-dist/dist is older than the deployed build
body:
Cloning `feature/linux-kernel-integration` and serving it with `./serve.sh` never reaches a shell. The kernel comes up and reaches PID 1, then init goes quiet:

```
[W:init (1)] start: vmlinux instantiated, invoking fn=62
[W:init (1)] switch_entry fn=616 arg=500772 ...
(nothing further — /tmp/wasm-kernel-debug.log stops growing)
```

next.linuxontab.com boots to a shell, so this is the committed tree rather than the code. The kernel is not the difference — `vmlinux.wasm` is byte-identical and everything around it is older:

```
                  committed    deployed
worker.js            72863       77869     (waliv=31 vs waliv=41)
wali-bridge.js       25163       27229
index.js             11591       12095
wasm.html           250288      257981
vmlinux.wasm       5310187     5310187     identical
```

Dropping only the deployed `dist/*.js` onto the committed `wasm.html` wedges the main thread, so those two look version-locked — the page seems to need the matching `dist/`.

Repro: fresh clone at a74368e, `./serve.sh 8765`, `/shell/wasm.html?debuglog&autoboot`. Chrome 153, Linux x86_64. Seen on three separate origins including your own serve.sh, and it is not a stale cache — a clean origin downloading the rootfs fresh does the same.

Separately, `shell/linux-dist/initramfs.cpio` has 12 bytes after the cpio trailer: `2029 blocks\n`, i.e. cpio's stderr, presumably a `2>&1` in whatever builds it. `head -c 1038848` on the committed file reproduces the deployed file's sha256 exactly. It is harmless to the boot, but it is what produces the misleading `Initramfs unpacking failed: invalid magic at start of compressed archive` line, which sent us a long way in the wrong direction.

On a happier note: `WispSlirp` needed no changes to run against a non-WebSocket WISP backend. We pointed it at a WISP server running inside the page over a virtual loopback, and guest TCP came out the far side normally. A PR follows with the small seam that makes that possible; `ws://`/`wss://` behaviour is unchanged.

title: fix wisp v2 spec bugs, add ci, tls, stream confirmation, and the wisp-tokio library
body:
<!-- ccr-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"devmidnightst"} -->
_Requested by **midnight** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01Qg87cDf6ZaoJMJFDz5MEZ4?thread=cmsg_01Qg87cDf6ZaoJMJFDz5MEZ4N8F73TiKQzg1vwRJFKPPpG)_

Before: `nyx-client` could not connect to `nyx-server` at all (`ResetWithoutClosingHandshake`), a slow upstream connect froze every stream on a websocket, flow control never applied backpressure, and upstream sockets leaked when the websocket dropped. There was no CI and no tests outside `wisp-core`. The server and client were single-purpose binaries, plain `ws://` only.

After: the client and server talk to each other and to MercuryWorkshop's wisp-js, in both directions. The protocol lives in a reusable async crate (`wisp-tokio`), the server can serve `wss://`, the stream open confirmation extension is supported, and CI builds, lints and runs 125 tests on every push and PR.

This PR is three rounds of work, one per commit group below.

## 1. spec fixes (`b6fc47f`)

**handshake**
- the client sends `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, and the server echoes back the first offered subprotocol. clients fail the upgrade without that echo
- without the header the server acts as a wisp v1 server, as the spec requires. it refuses v1 when auth is required

**auth**
- either offered method is enough when both are enabled
- a client with no credentials gets `0xc2`
- the client sends CLOSE on stream 0 before rejecting a server
- usernames over 255 bytes are rejected instead of wrapping

**mux**
- a slow upstream connect no longer blocks the reader loop
- DATA sent before the connect finishes is queued instead of dropped
- CONTINUE is counted on write, and queues are bounded, so flow control applies real backpressure. a client that overruns its window is closed with `0x49`
- upstream sockets close when the websocket drops
- stream id reuse no longer lets an old task tear down the new stream
- UDP to ipv6 destinations works
- socket errors report `0x03` instead of `0x02`

**misc**
- `--buffer-size 0` is rejected
- the client accepts `[ipv6]:port` targets
- `Cargo.lock` is tracked

## 2. ci and tests (`aac68ae`, `0d831a6`)
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs build, clippy with `-D warnings` and tests, with `--locked`
- end to end tests against the real `nyx-server` binary. 20 of the original 21 fail on `main`
- boxed tungstenite's error type so the newer clippy on CI passes

## 3. protocol features and the library (`982da29`)

**`wisp-tokio` (new crate)**
- `server::accept(socket, Arc<ServerConfig>)` works over any `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`. the mux moved here from `nyx-server` unchanged apart from being generic, plus the features below
- `client::ClientMux` runs the handshake and spawns a driver task. `open_tcp` / `open_udp` return `WispStream`, which implements `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite`, waits on the CONTINUE window, and closes on shutdown or drop. `send_packet` / `recv_packet` keep UDP datagram boundaries
- close reasons map to `io::ErrorKind`s, so connection refused, timeouts and so on read naturally
- password comparison is constant time

**stream open confirmation (extension 0x05)**
- offered by default. TCP streams get a CONTINUE once the upstream socket connects, and UDP never gets one (the spec forbids it)
- the confirmation window subtracts packets the client already sent early, and the per-stream queue holds two windows, so a client that raced ahead is never wrongly throttled
- `ClientMux::open` waits for the confirmation, so a refused connect comes back from `open` as an error

**nyx-server**
- `--tls-cert` / `--tls-key` for `wss://` (rustls with the ring provider, ALPN `http/1.1`)
- `--no-udp`, `--no-stream-confirmation`, `--connect-timeout`, and `--handshake-timeout`. before this, a silent client could hold a connection open forever

**nyx-client**
- runs on the library
- supports `wss://`, with web PKI roots plus an optional `--ca-cert`
- prints readable errors

## testing
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked` with `-D warnings`: clean
- `cargo test --workspace`: 125 passing (45 core unit, 20 library unit, 18 library integration, 32 server e2e, 3 client unit, 6 client binary, 1 doctest). 3 full runs in a row were all green
- interop with `@mercuryworkshop/wisp-js` 0.5.0:
  - its client pushed a 3 MiB echo through `nyx-server --buffer-size 8`
  - `nyx-client` pushed 2 MB of random bytes through `wisp-js-server`, byte for byte

## not changed (worth a look)
- the server still connects anywhere a client asks, loopback and private ranges included. that's an SSRF risk on a public deploy, left for a separate decision
- the repo isn't rustfmt clean, so CI doesn't check formatting yet

title: feat(transport): HyperDHT in the web app and the extension, through a relay
body:
Brings HyperDHT (WISP 103) to the web app and the extension, through a HyperDHT relay (Holepunch's `@hyperswarm/dht-relay`). Phase 1 (spike) is done and the answer is **go**, with three upstream bugs fixed on our side. Phase 2 (implementation) is in progress below.

## Spike report (phase 1)

### Security: where the crypto ends
- **dht-relay's client is custodial by default.** It sends the browser's **secret key** to the relay in its handshake, connect and listen messages, and the relay then runs Noise and the secret stream for it. That would be a no-go.
- **Non-custodial mode (`custodial: false`) keeps everything at the endpoint**, and it is the only mode we use.
  - The browser holds its keypair and runs the Noise IK handshake itself. The relay only forwards the handshake messages.
  - The browser runs the `SecretStream` over the relayed raw bytes. The relay forwards ciphertext.
  - The browser signs its own DHT announcements (the relay asks it for each signature).
  - Checked by capturing everything the browser sent to the relay: no plaintext, no secret key, no handshake hash (unit test `hyperdhtRelay.test.ts`).
- **The WISP 103 binding is unchanged.** It is still the Noise handshake hash plus both keys, computed at each endpoint. Browser and Desktop compute the same binding, so pinning and the transcript work as on any transport.
- **What the relay sees:**
  - the browser's IP address;
  - the HyperDHT public keys it listens on and dials (per-chat transport keys, not participation keys);
  - timing and sizes of the traffic;
  - the holepunch secret and stream id, which are hashes of the handshake and not the session keys.
- **One residual point.** For an incoming stream, dht-relay's client takes the peer's public key from the relay's message. A lying relay would put a wrong key in the binding. The Ghostly transcript then differs at the two ends, so the pairing fails; it can't impersonate anyone. That is the same power a relay already has (it can drop bytes). I left this unpatched (see "patches" below).

### Upstream bugs (dht-relay 0.4.3, the latest release, from 2023) and a browser gap
1. **Relayed listen was broken on hyperdht 6.x.** The relay passes the announce record where the client expects its relay-address list, so every announce signature throws and nobody can reach a listening browser. Fixed in our relay (`native-transports/hyperdht-relay/relay.mjs`).
2. **One client could crash the relay.** When an incoming stream fails, the relay sends a `destroy` message it can't encode, and the throw comes out of an event handler, taking the whole process down. Fixed in our relay: the message is corrected, and any unsendable message drops that one client.
3. **Leak.** When a listening browser leaves, the relay closes its server, whose unannounce waits forever for that browser's signature. Fixed: a signature comes within 10 s, or while the browser is still connected.
4. **Browser crypto gap.** `sodium-javascript`, the browser build of sodium-universal, lacks `crypto_scalarmult_ed25519_noclamp`, the operation HyperDHT's Noise curve runs on. The handshake hangs on its first message. Fixed with `packages/browser/src/platform/noiseCurveEd.ts` on `@noble/curves`, swapped in for `noise-curve-ed` by the browser builds. It is equal to libsodium on random keys (unit test against sodium-native), and refuses the same inputs: small-order, non-canonical and mixed-order points.

No patch-package: the web Docker image installs with `--ignore-scripts`, so all fixes live in our code.

### Proven
- **Chromium ↔ Desktop.** A real Chromium page loads the bundled client and talks to the Desktop's own `endpoint.mjs` both ways; both ends compute the same binding.
- **web ↔ web** on one relay, and across two relays.
- **A whole `GhostLink` paired chat** between two relayed browsers with WebRTC off: handshake, pin, messages (unit test).

### Numbers (Miguel's Mac; relay and Desktop endpoint on the Mac, both behind its NAT)

| | runs | connect p50 | max | listen (announce) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chromium → Desktop, **public** HyperDHT | 9/10 (1 timed out at 30 s) | 1.18 s | 2.0 s | ~2.7 s |
| Chromium ↔ Chromium, one relay, **public** HyperDHT | 10/10 | 1.35 s | 2.2 s | ~2.0 s |
| web ↔ web, two relays, local testnet | 20/20 | 7 ms | 9 ms | |
| Chromium → Desktop, local testnet | 1/1 | 61 ms | | |

- **Against WebRTC.** WebRTC loopback connects in ~40 ms (#225's measurement). Across NATs it depends on STUN/TURN. A relayed HyperDHT dial is ~1.2-1.4 s on the public DHT, and every byte crosses the relay, so it is a **fallback**, never first. Hence the ranking rule below.
- **Bundle.** 474 KB minified / 107 KB gzip, as a lazy chunk loaded only when a relay is configured and a chat starts its endpoint (noble ed25519 is shared with the app).

### MV3 extension
- The engine runs in the offscreen document, a normal extension page with `WebSocket`. The service worker isn't involved.
- The manifest's `extension_pages` CSP sets no `connect-src`, so `wss://` is allowed.

### CSPs
- **Web (nginx):** `connect-src https: wss:` already covers a TLS relay.
- **Desktop:** no change; it keeps the native sidecar.
- **Development/e2e:** the adapter accepts `ws://` only to loopback.

### Who runs the relay (needs Miguel's OK, not deployed)
- **Nobody runs a public dht-relay for us.** Proposal: a `ghostly-hyperdht-relay` container on "zero" behind the Cloudflare tunnel, as `wss://hyperdht-relay.ghostly.tools`. Node, ~60-100 MB RAM, a 256 MB memory limit, 0.25 CPU.
- **Abuse limits (in the relay):**
  - 512 clients in total, 16 per address (`CF-Connecting-IP` behind the tunnel);
  - 256 KiB per message;
  - 512 KiB/s per client, 4 MiB burst (the relay pauses the socket past that);
  - 16 listens per client, 60 dials per minute;
  - topic lookups and announcements refused (no open crawler);
  - an optional `Origin` allowlist (app.ghostly.tools + the extension).
- **Cost:** bandwidth, since every byte of a relayed chat crosses the relay.
- **Default until then: off** (no relay URL). The URL is configurable in Settings.

### Go/no-go
**Go.** Security holds in non-custodial mode, the Desktop interoperates unchanged, and reliability is 29/30 on the public DHT with ~1.2 s dials. The bugs found are fixed on our side and covered by tests.

## Phase 2 (done)
- [x] Relay server `native-transports/hyperdht-relay`:
  - the fixes above, the limits, `/healthz`, a testnet mode for e2e;
  - Dockerfile and a proposed compose file (512 MB, 0.5 CPU, read-only);
  - measured: 46 MB idle, 100 MB with 100 browsers listening, 182 MB after 50 MiB through it in 2.2 s.
- [x] `hyperdht/1` browser `NativeEndpoint` (`platform/hyperdhtRelay.ts`):
  - one WebSocket per relay, shared by every chat, lazy-loaded;
  - the descriptor is `{publicKey, relayed: true, relay}`.
- [x] `noise-curve-ed` replacement for browser builds (vite plugin), with equivalence tests against libsodium.
- [x] **Rank: rebased onto #225's `relayed` flag** (it landed first and owns it; same semantics as the spike proposed). HyperDHT's relayed descriptor feeds #225's `relayedTransports` and `relayedPath`, so its panel names the HyperDHT relay too.
- [x] **Settings, Network: "HyperDHT relay (optional)".**
  - Accepts `wss://`, or `ws://` to this machine; **off by default** until Miguel decides on hosting.
  - A new URL moves idle chats to it; the app listens again 30 s after the relay drops.
- [x] **Shown:**
  - the popover and summary use #225's "Relayed via host";
  - the header menu says "relayed";
  - the options say "Through a relay · used when nothing direct connects";
  - the timeline says "Moved to HyperDHT, through a relay" (never "a direct path was found").
- [x] WISP 103 revision 0.3 (browser profile: non-custodial, what the relay sees, crypto, bugs). WISP 100: #225's relayed section now covers HyperDHT.
- [x] e2e/infra:
  - `ghostly-e2e-hyperdht-relay` on 47097, on its own HyperDHT testnet, running on "one";
  - `infra.mjs add <service>` starts a new service on a shared stack without seeding.
- [x] e2e `web/hyperdht-relay.spec.ts` (`@gated`): two browsers pair, set the relay, lose WebRTC entirely (no `RTCPeerConnection`) and chat live over HyperDHT through the relay. It passed 5/5 locally, plus the iroh-relay, transport-timeline and network-settings specs.
- [x] Unit tests:
  - the adapter against the real relay and the Desktop's `endpoint.mjs`: binding, secrets never on the relay's wire, limits, relay gone;
  - the engine settings/factory;
  - the UI wording;
  - the switch rank with a relayed HyperDHT.

## Open (needs Miguel)
- **Hosting and default.** The proposal is a relay on "zero" as `wss://hyperdht-relay.ghostly.tools`; then set `DEFAULT_HYPERDHT_RELAY`. Nothing is deployed.
- **First contact.** It still takes WebRTC: the browser learns the contact's HyperDHT key inside a session. #209's capability record has `descriptors: {}` today; putting the relayed key there would let a first contact use HyperDHT.
- **Shared stack on "one".** An old checkout running a full `e2e:infra:up` with `--remove-orphans` would drop services it doesn't know (both relays). `up` on a running stack just joins, so this only bites on a fresh start.

title: feat(transport): Iroh in the web app and the extension, through a relay
body:
Brings Iroh (WISP 102) to the web app and the extension, through an Iroh relay. Phase 1 (spike) is done and the answer is **go**. Phase 2 (implementation) is in progress below.

## Spike report (phase 1)

**What was built.** `native-transports/iroh-web` compiles **iroh 1.2.0**, the exact version the Desktop pins, for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Iroh has an official browser mode (`wasm_browser`): no UDP, so every packet goes through an Iroh relay over a WebSocket. The QUIC/TLS session is still end to end between the two endpoints, so the relay sees IPs and timing, never frames. The crate reuses the Desktop's wire exactly: ALPN `ghostly/paired-chat/1`, the stream preface, u32 length-prefixed text frames up to 60 KiB, and the same TLS exporter (`EXPORTER-Ghostly-paired-chat-v1`). `scripts/build-iroh-web.mjs` builds it into `packages/iroh-web/pkg` (`@ghostly/iroh-web`). The output is committed, so the web/extension/Docker builds need no Rust. `packages/browser/src/platform/irohWeb.ts` is a `NativeEndpoint` over it, the same interface the Desktop's Tauri bridge implements.

**Proven** (`packages/browser/test/irohWeb.test.ts`, runs when `IROH_RELAY_URL` is set):
- web↔web: two browser endpoints run the whole core paired handshake (pin, binding check, messages, a 16 KiB message) through a local `iroh-relay` 1.2.0.
- web↔Desktop: a browser endpoint and the native `iroh-peer` (the Desktop's Rust wire code) pair both ways, whichever side dials.
- Same native binding: both sides compute the same 32-byte exporter context and the same sorted identities, so pinning and the rank sum work unchanged.
- Real Chromium (Playwright, a page with the production CSP shape `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'`) connects through the local relay and through n0's public relays, including the trailing-dot relay URLs (`https://use1-1.relay.n0.iroh.link./`) the Desktop publishes.

**Numbers** (Miguel's Mac, Chromium headless unless noted)

| | wasm load | online (relay) | connect | frame RTT (median) | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Iroh, local relay | 10 ms | 0.23 s | 24 ms (paired handshake: 48 ms) | 0.3 ms | 12.5 MiB/s |
| Iroh, n0 relay `use1` | | 1.9 s | 0.49 s | 290 ms | 1.3 MiB/s |
| Iroh, n0 relay `euc1` | | 2.3 s | 0.63 s | 378 ms | 1.0 MiB/s |
| WebRTC loopback, same page | | | 42 ms | 0.2 ms | 5.0 MiB/s (naive harness) |

A relayed path costs two client-to-relay round trips per frame round trip, and n0's shared relays cap throughput at about 1 MiB/s. That is fine for chat, files and payments, and too slow to beat a direct WebRTC path. Hence the "relayed" rank rule below.

**Bundle.** 2.89 MB wasm (1.08 MB gzip, 0.82 MB brotli) + 49 KB JS glue (9 KB gzip). It loads only when a chat starts an Iroh endpoint, never on the app's first load. For scale, the web build already lazy-loads Breez 12.8 MB, Fedimint 11.5 MB, Bark 7.7 MB and BDK 2.1 MB of wasm. `opt-level = "z"` saves only 60 KB gzip, so the crate keeps `s`.

**MV3 extension.** The engine runs in the offscreen document, a normal extension page with WebSocket and wasm. The manifest's `extension_pages` CSP already has `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` and sets no `connect-src`, so relay WebSockets are allowed. No service-worker involvement.

**CSPs.** Web (nginx): `script-src 'wasm-unsafe-eval'` and `connect-src https: wss:` already cover a TLS relay. Desktop: Iroh stays native, no change. Extension: see above.

**Relay decision.** The default is **n0's public relays**, the same ones the Desktop's Iroh already homes on (`presets::N0`). This needs no new infrastructure and keeps web↔Desktop on shared relays. Relay URLs are configurable. Self-hosting `iroh-relay` on "zero" is recommended for production traffic (n0 rate-limits its public relays), but it needs Miguel's OK and is not part of this PR. e2e uses a local `iroh-relay` in the shared infra (`ghostly-e2e-iroh-relay`).

**Limit found.** First contact still needs WebRTC or the DHT: a browser learns a contact's Iroh id and relay only over an authenticated session today. The one-chat capability record (#209) carries them on the DHT, so its part 2 can dial Iroh from the first contact.

## Phase 2 (implemented)
- [x] `@ghostly/iroh-web` package + `scripts/build-iroh-web.mjs` (iroh 1.2.0 = Desktop, wasm-bindgen 0.2.106). wasm-bindgen output is not byte-reproducible, so `pkg/BUILD.json` records a hash of the crate's sources and of the wasm, and `scripts/test/irohWebBuild.test.ts` fails when the crate changes without a rebuild, the pkg is edited, or the browser iroh drifts from the Desktop's.
- [x] Web host and extension offscreen peer run it (`NodeOptions.irohWeb`). It loads on the first chat that starts an endpoint and is advertised only once its relay answers. The Desktop build aliases `@ghostly/iroh-web` to a 178-byte stub, so no wasm ships in the app.
- [x] **Relayed rank flag** (`packages/core/src/pairedTransports.ts`): `relayedTransports(local, remote)` marks a transport as relayed when either side's descriptor has `relayed: true` (or an Iroh descriptor has no address). `rankTransports(local, remote, relayed)` puts relayed transports after every direct one, symmetric from both sides. Used by `GhostLink.dial` and `TransportSwitch.choices`. An explicit choice still wins, and a live relayed session is kept (no probing while live, WISP 100).
- [x] **Fallback after WebRTC**: when the dialling side's WebRTC attempt ends without opening (fails at once, or ICE times out), it goes on to the next ranked transports (a relayed Iroh) before the DHT floor. Allow fallback off on either side skips it.
- [x] Indicator + panel: "Connected · Iroh (relayed)", `data-relayed`, a "Path: Relayed via <relay hosts>" row, "relayed" in the tooltip and menu line (`LinkView.transportRelayed`).
- [x] Settings, Network: Iroh relay URLs (browsers only; https, or http on loopback; at most 4; empty = n0 defaults). Idle endpoints re-home when it changes.
- [x] CSP: no change needed (web `connect-src https: wss:` + `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`; extension has no connect-src limit; Desktop stays native).
- [x] WISP 100 rev 0.3 ("Relayed transports") and WISP 102 rev 0.3 ("Browser profile: relay only", with the measurements). Website reference data re-synced.
- [x] e2e infra: `ghostly-e2e-iroh-relay` (`n0computer/iroh-relay:v1.2.0 --dev`) on 47085, `GHOSTLY_IROH_RELAY_URL`. On "one" it was added alone (`infra.mjs up --host one` now starts only missing services when the chain answers, no re-seed).

## Tests
- `packages/core/test/relayedTransports.test.ts`: detection, rank with the flag (every permutation symmetric, direct before relayed), switch keeps direct, keeps relayed live, relayed last among fallbacks, explicit choice of relayed stands.
- `packages/browser/test/relayedFallback.test.ts`: two real `GhostLink`s, WebRTC throwing / never answering → relayed Iroh; fallback off → no Iroh.
- `packages/browser/test/irohWeb.test.ts` (gated on `GHOSTLY_IROH_RELAY_URL`): the real wasm in Node, web↔web and web↔native `iroh-peer` pairing, both dial directions, through the infra relay.
- e2e `e2e/web/iroh-relay.spec.ts`: web↔web, pair over WebRTC, block WebRTC in both pages, reconnect lands on relayed Iroh, messages both ways, panel names the relay; bad relay URL refused, reset to defaults. `e2e/extension/iroh-relay.spec.ts`: extension (offscreen) ↔ web moved onto relayed Iroh from the Connection menu (MV3 proof). Both pass against the relay on "one". `transport-timeline`, `pairing-extras`, `network-settings`, `settings`, `menus`, `extension/interop` re-run green.
- Fixtures keep Iroh off by default (`ghostly-test-iroh=off` for web, a closed local port for the extension) so the suite stays offline and specs written for a WebRTC-only browser hold. `peer(name, { irohRelay })` opts in.
- Features: `transport.iroh-web`, `transport.relayed`, `settings.network.iroh-relays`, infra `iroh-relay`.

## Not in this PR
- Web↔Desktop in e2e: Linux WebKitGTK Desktop has no WebRTC for the first pairing, and descriptors come only from a session. This is covered in-process by the native `iroh-peer` test above. #209 part 2 (descriptors in the capability record) unlocks first contact over Iroh.
- The Desktop keeps n0's relays; the relay setting applies to browsers.
- A self-hosted relay on "zero" needs Miguel's OK.
- Found in passing, pre-existing: Settings, Network reopened within 50 ms of a save shows the old values (the engine coalesces state broadcasts).

title: feat(nostr): the social layer on top of a Nostr proof — profile, follows, notes, publication
body:
## What

The **Nostr social layer** on top of the Nostr identity proof (WISP 300/301): what a proven Nostr key lets a person **show** and **do**, as separate, separately permitted capabilities, following the roadmap's "Identity, profiles and social data" table (proof ≠ profile ≠ social graph ≠ content ≠ publication). Draft: [`docs/wisps/3xx-nostr-social.md`](docs/wisps/3xx-nostr-social.md).

| Layer | What ships | Permission |
|---|---|---|
| Profile (kind 0) | name, handle, about, NIP-05, website, picture; cached with the relays that answered, fetch time, the event's time/id, stale after a day | "Load profile", or the explicit *auto-load* setting (off) |
| Social graph (kind 3) | whom the contact follows; hints against the person's own list: *follows you*, *you follow them*, *you both follow N*, each labelled with its direction and time | "Load follows" + "Load mine"; nothing inferred as trusted |
| Content (kind 1) | the contact's notes, newest first, paginated (`until`), at most 200 kept, hidden by the person's own kind-10000 mute list (public `p`/`e`/`word`) | "Load notes" / "Older notes"; no feed, no ranking |
| Publication (kinds 1, 3, 0) | post a note, follow/unfollow, update the profile | a capability **off by default**; each action drafted by the engine, shown with a "public on Nostr" notice naming the relays, confirmed, signed by the person's **own** NIP-07/NIP-46 signer (never a stored key), checked against the draft before it is sent |

## Where

- **Profile → Nostr** (shown once the profile has a Nostr key or a contact shared one): relays (defaults shown, editable, `wss://` only, ≤ 8), the two switches, and per own key: profile, follow count, mute-list summary, *Post a note*, *Update profile*.
- **Chat → Identities**, under a verified Nostr proof: the contact card (profile, hints, notes, *Follow/Unfollow on Nostr*). The proof card takes the loaded name and picture with its source. The old provider `lookupDisplay` for Nostr now goes through this layer, so it uses the person's relays instead of two fixed ones.

## Privacy rules, as built

- Nothing is asked about a key the contact did not prove (verified, not expired/withdrawn/revoked); what was loaded for a key that stops being verified is dropped at once.
- Nothing is fetched or published without the person's action or the explicit setting; every place that fetches says which relays learn the IP address and the key.
- Relays are only the person's list: nothing discovers relays from what it reads (kind-3 relay lists, NIP-65, tag hints).
- Every event is checked on a copy (strict shape, bounds, id recomputed, BIP-340), replaceable kinds newest-wins per NIP-01; text is plain and capped; pictures only from the fixed hosts of PUBLIC-PROFILES, re-encoded small; a manual chat name always wins.
- A kind 3 / kind 0 is rebuilt from the current event read fresh from the relays so nothing else is dropped; if no relay answers, the app refuses to publish a replacement blind.

## Tests

- Unit (`packages/browser/test/nostrSocial.test.ts`, `nostrSocialEngine.test.ts`, 27 tests): parsing and bounds of kinds 0/3/1/10000, mute rules, follow hints, templates (follow keeps every other tag and the legacy content; profile keeps unknown fields), relay URL rules, the relay client against a relay in the test process (EOSE, oversize frame, no EOSE, budget, abort, OK/refusals), and the engine module: refused without a verified proof or offline, cache with provenance and staleness, hints once own list is loaded, pagination, mute, dropped when the proof goes, auto-load only with the setting, publication gating, draft binding (other key / altered event / unknown draft refused before anything is sent).
- E2E (`e2e/web/nostr-social.spec.ts`): three people, a Nostr relay inside the test process (`e2e/support/nostrRelay.ts`, Playwright routes the WebSocket, no port), a NIP-07 signer injected in the page with a disposable key. The contact without the proof sees no card and asks no relay; the other loads the profile with picture, follows with hints, notes with one hidden by the mute list; then turns publication on and posts a note, updates the profile and unfollows/follows, with the relay receiving exactly those events and the signer asked exactly that many times.
- `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (802 passed) and the identity-proof and responsive e2e specs pass locally.

## Docs

WISP draft `3xx-nostr-social.md` (registered in `numbering.json`, the website's synced copies regenerated), roadmap layer table and Nostr row updated, catalogue and numbering rows, 301 follow-up, PROOFS.md provider row, PUBLIC-PROFILES note, e2e README row.

## Not included

Reactions, replies/mentions, DMs, deletion requests (NIP-09), NIP-65 relay lists, the mute list's private part, publishing a mute list. The profile name is never used as the chat's name.

title: wisp: run a session over any transport, so it works on js/wasm
body:
pkg/wisp did not build for js/wasm, and could not have worked there:

```
pkg/wisp/client.go: unknown field HTTPClient in websocket.DialOptions
vendor/github.com/coder/websocket/accept.go:1: //go:build !js
```

The client failed to compile because the js build wraps the page's own WebSocket, whose `DialOptions` carry a subprotocol list and nothing else. The server was worse: **`websocket.Accept` does not exist on js at all**, so a Wisp server could not be created in a tab. And a service worker cannot intercept `ws://` or `wss://`, so a page-served endpoint could not have been reached even if it existed.

Nothing in a session needs a WebSocket — it reads a frame, writes a frame, and closes. `Frames` names that, and `streamFrames` carries a session over any `net.Conn` by length-prefixing each frame, so a visor in a tab can serve Wisp on a virtual-loopback port. `Server.ServeConn` and `DialConn` are the entry points; `ServeHTTP` is unchanged and now sits behind `//go:build !js` with the rest of the WebSocket path.

`HTTPClient` and `Header` stay in `ClientConfig` on every platform and are **refused, not ignored**, where a browser cannot honor them — silently dropping a proxy the caller asked for would send the traffic straight out of the page, the exact thing they were avoiding. The error names `DialConn`.

One behavioural difference is handled rather than inherited: a WebSocket read abandons itself when its context is canceled and a byte-stream read does not, so `ServeFrames` turns cancellation into a close.

The harness moved to `harness_test.go` untagged, and socket-dependent tests are `//go:build !js`, so the transport-agnostic ones **run under a real js/wasm runtime**. They do — a whole session (TCP echo, UDP datagrams, 400 KiB through the credit window) passes under node via `go_js_wasm_exec`, which is a stronger claim than compiling.

The WebSocket path is unchanged on the wire and was re-checked live: CONNECT 200, and three DNS queries through UDP ASSOCIATE over a real exit. `go test -count=3 -race ./pkg/wisp/` clean at 80.2% coverage; golangci-lint 0 issues.

title: feat: 接続 QR コードをカメラでコピーできる形に作り直す
body:
## 概要

nostter からスキャンした接続 QR コードのテキストをコピーできず、リモート署名に接続できない不具合（#460）に対応する。実装プランは [issue #460 のコメント](https://github.com/neverclear86/nostr-no-su/issues/460#issuecomment-5776890341)のとおり。`bunker://` を先頭に持つ文字列は Android と iPad の標準カメラがスキームを知らない URL として扱いコピーできないため、接続 QR コードのページの既定を「`bunker://` を外し `relay=` のドットを `%2E` にしたコピー用の QR」に作り直し、従来どおりの完全な `bunker://` URI の QR はアプリ内スキャナー向けに畳みへ移した。

## 変更点

### `src/nostr_no_su/bunker/account.gleam`
`bunker_uri` の出力から `bunker://` を外し `relay=` の値のドットを `%2E` に置き換える `camera_copy_text` を追加した。

### `src/nostr_no_su/admin/account_pages.gleam`
接続 QR コードのページ（`connection_qr_page`）を作り直した。各カードの既定をコピー用の QR・貼り方の案内・コピー欄にし、完全な `bunker://` URI の QR は畳みへ移した。要承認のカードには承認待ちの節へのリンクを、ページ末尾にはバンカーが使うリレーの一覧とクライアント側 URI での接続経路の案内を足した。

### `src/nostr_no_su/admin/dashboard.gleam`
承認待ちの節のアンカー定数 `pending_anchor` を `pub` にした（接続 QR コードのページからのリンクが参照する）。

### `src/nostr_no_su/admin/view.gleam`
等幅の 1 行を並べる箇条書きの部品 `code_list` を追加した。

### `src/nostr_no_su/admin/i18n.gleam`
文言を 8 件追加し、`ConnectionQrDescription` と `ConnectionQrSecretWarning` を新しい画面構成に合わせて差し替えた。

### `priv/static/admin.css`
`code_list` が使う Tailwind のクラスを反映して再ビルドした。

### `docs/usage.md` / `docs/admin-ui.md` / `docs/design-decisions.md`
新しい画面構成に文書を追随させ、`design-decisions.md` に QR コードを 2 通り出す設計判断を追記した。

### `test/account_test.gleam` / `test/admin_accounts_test.gleam` / `test/i18n_test.gleam` / `test/japanese_pages_test.gleam`
`camera_copy_text` と新しい画面構成のテストを追加し、`next_message` の鎖・件数・`allowed_words` を追随させた。

## テストと検証

### 検証の手順（プランの番号に対応）

1. `git -C <作業ツリー> status --porcelain && env -C <作業ツリー> gleam test 2>&1 | tail -1`: `1048 passed, no failures`（`COVERAGE=1 TEST_DATABASE_URL=... gleam test` で実行。`coverage: 4947/5434 lines (91.0%)`、`sh dev/check_coverage_badge.sh` は差分無し）

4. 撮影用サーバー（`PREVIEW_PORT=5901`）で日英・w1280/w375・light/dark を撮影した。`node dev/screenshots.mjs` は `28b-approve-page-pending-unavailable`（本 PR と無関係な既存の画面）で 503 を返し `ja-ok` / `en-ok` は出なかったが、origin/main を同じ手順で撮っても同じ 503 が再現するため既存の flake であり本 PR の対象外。`18b-connection-qr-*.png` は日英とも 4 枚ずつ撮れている
5. 撮影した 8 枚を目視で確認した。カードの上の QR の下に手順の 1 文と注記の 1 文が出ている。畳みは閉じた状態で summary が 1 行に収まっている。`w375` で QR とリレーの URL が横にはみ出さない。light と dark の両方で文字が読める。要承認のカードに承認待ちへのリンクが出ている。うち `18b-connection-qr-w1280-light`（日英）と `-w375-light`（日本語）を本 PR に貼った
6. 実機での読み取りとコピーはユーザーが確認済みである（issue #460 のやり取りで、`bunker://` を外し `relay=` のドットを `%2E` にした形は Android 15 と iPad の標準カメラのどちらでもテキストとしてコピーできた）。貼った後に接続まで進むかは別の要因（リレーへの到達性、承認、secret の作り直し）に依存し、この PR の対象外である（「後続の作業」）

### 掃き出した語

- `sh dev/sweep_refs.sh <作業ツリー> ConnectionQrDescription ConnectionQrSecretWarning CouldNotEncodeQr connection_qr_page`: いずれも既存の参照のみ
- `sh dev/sweep_refs.sh <作業ツリー> code_list ScanWithCamera CameraCopyIntro BunkerRelaysForUri camera_copy_text pending_anchor`: `ScanWithCamera`・`CameraCopyIntro` は 0 件（プランが避けた名前と衝突なし）
- `sh dev/sweep_refs.sh <作業ツリー> ScanWithClientScanner CameraCopySteps CameraCopyNote BunkerRelaysForUri BunkerRelaysHint ApprovalUriNeedsApproval ConnectWithClientUri ConnectWithClientUriHint camera_copy_text code_list bunker_relay_card client_uri_card approval_note pending_anchor`: rebase 後に再実行、想定どおりの定義・呼び出し箇所のみ
- `git grep -n "QR" docs/ README.md README.ja.md` / `git grep -n "読み取り機能" docs/`: README.md・README.ja.md は 0 件、docs/architecture.md の QR の記述はルートとファイル名のみで変更対象外

掃き出した語: `ConnectionQrDescription`、`ConnectionQrSecretWarning`、`CouldNotEncodeQr`、`connection_qr_page`、`code_list`、`ScanWithCamera`、`CameraCopyIntro`、`BunkerRelaysForUri`、`camera_copy_text`、`pending_anchor`、`ScanWithClientScanner`、`CameraCopySteps`、`CameraCopyNote`、`BunkerRelaysHint`、`ApprovalUriNeedsApproval`、`ConnectWithClientUri`、`ConnectWithClientUriHint`、`bunker_relay_card`、`client_uri_card`、`approval_note`、`QR`（docs/README）、`読み取り機能`（docs）

### `dev/check_plan_tests.sh` の突き合わせ

プランのテスト 8 件はすべて実装にある。

## プランからの変更

実装時の条件として指示された 4 点を取り込んだ。
1. `ConnectWithClientUriHint` の日本語は「管理 UI」ではなく「管理画面」を使う指定どおりの全文にした（`UI` が `japanese_pages_have_no_english_words_test` の `allowed_words` に無いため）。
2. 承認待ちへのリンクの文言は新規の `Message` を足さず、既存の `i18n.PendingConnections` をそのまま使った。
3. 検証の手順 6 を、実機確認済みの旨を PR 本文に 1 行で書く形に差し替えた（上の「テストと検証」に記載）。
4. `docs/admin-ui.md` に、要承認のカードが承認待ちの節へのリンクを添える旨の 1 文を「続けて、」の直前に挿んだ。

このほか、要承認のカードの note（承認待ちへの案内とリンク）をプランは `uri_card` の呼び出し側に直接書く形で示していたが、実装では `approval_note` という小さいヘルパーに切り出した（`uri_card` の呼び出し側の見通しを保つため。中身はプランの指示どおり）。

title: Memories ("On this day"): own kind-1 notes from this day 1/2/3 years back
body:
## Memories ("On this day")

Port of Android `MemoriesRepository` / `MemoriesCard` / `MemoriesScreen` / `MemoriesViewModel`: the signed-in user's OWN kind-1 notes from this same calendar day 1, 2, and 3 years ago. Read-only — no new event kind, nothing published, so §7.13 does not apply.

Two entry points: a dismissible teaser card in the feed (self-hiding when dismissed or when there is nothing today) and a drawer row ("Memories", next to My Polls) to the full screen, presented as a sheet like `PollsView`.

### What landed
- **`wisp/Memories.swift`** — pure top-level helpers, testable without a relay or a view:
  - `memoryWindows(now:calendar:)` — local-time day bounds in the USER's time zone; Feb 29 → Feb 28 in non-leap target years.
  - `isMemoryReply(_:)` — the corrected NIP-10 predicate: a reply iff any **non-empty-id** `e` tag lacks a **case-insensitive** `mention` marker. Mention-only `e` tags and `q` quotes are not replies. Deliberately not `NostrEvent.hasThreadingETag` / `Nip10` (see #86).
  - `shouldCacheMemories(_:)` — **the rule not to get wrong:** cache only when EVERY window resolved via EOSE. An EOSE'd window with zero notes IS cacheable ("nothing that day"); a timed-out window is not, because no relay finished its scan. Android learned this by freezing the 3-year window empty for users who had notes there. Ported with its reasoning verbatim; a stored partial also reads as a miss.
  - `memoriesLocalDateKey(now:calendar:)`.
  - `MemoriesStore` — `UserDefaults` on the `SocialGraphCache` pattern: `memories_v1_<pubkey>` (JSON data) and `memories_dismissed_<pubkey>` (today's date key); injected defaults. **v1**, not Android's v2 — their bump exists only to abandon caches poisoned by the partial-result bug, which iOS never shipped.
  - `MemoriesRelay` — union `RelayDefaults.defaults` ∪ `wss://nostr.wine`, with the **2026-09-19 retention measurement** in the comment (primal returned zero at one year, not just "past three"; damus 503s; eden AUTH-gates). Budgets: 8 s connect + 10/12/14 s EOSE by depth + 4 s grace after a real EOSE only; window limit 50; replies and empty-content notes excluded; oldest first.
  - `MemoriesSubSeq` — process-wide subId sequence (§7.2); CLOSE goes only to the subId actually opened on the relays it was opened on via `RelayConnectionPool.deregister` (§7.5).
  - `MemoriesRepository` — cache-first `getMemoriesCached`, cache-bypassing `refreshMemories` (overwrites only when authoritative), per-day dismissal, and in-flight coalescing so the card and the screen mounting together share one relay round.
- **`wisp/MemoriesCard.swift`** — teaser under `FeedLiveNowSection` in **both** feed bodies via `FeedTabRouting.showsMemoriesTeaser(for:)`. Deliberate and documented in code: Memories surfaces the user's own notes whatever their topic, so a non-food memory can appear on OnlyFood — a knowing inconsistency, justified because OnlyFood is the default landing. Renders nothing on a day with no memories. ✕ dismisses for the day with a 5 s Undo.
- **`wisp/MemoriesView.swift` + `MemoriesViewModel.swift`** — the full screen: header with today's date, groups "1 year ago / 2 years ago / 3 years ago" with the date, per-group empty text, notes through the shared `PostCardView`, Refresh in the toolbar with "Couldn't refresh — showing cached memories." when a window times out. Taps hand typed routes back to the feed stack (same hand-off as `PollsView`).
- `MainView.swift` / `SidebarDrawerView.swift` / `wisp/FeedTabRouting.swift` wiring; `.gitignore` entry for the live enable file.

### Tests (+37, 897 vs 860 on main)
- `MemoriesTests` (36): windows incl. Jan 1, Dec 31, Feb 29 fallback, Feb 28 stays, NY-vs-Tokyo boundaries; reply predicate incl. `Mention`/`MENTION`, `q` quotes, bare `["e"]`, `["e", ""]`, mention+reply; cache rule incl. the frozen-3-year case and a timeout WITH events; date key; store round trip / stored-partial-as-miss / per-day dismissal; repository gating with an injected fetch (complete → one relay round per day; partial → shown, not cached, re-fetched next open; refresh keeps cache when not authoritative; concurrent opens coalesce; subIds unique across instances). Two control assertions pin the shared helper's current wrong behaviour for #86 to flip.
- `MemoriesLiveTests` (1, opt-in, read-only): fetches real memories and prints per-window count + EOSE/TIMEOUT.

### Local results (Air, 2026-09-19)
- `build-for-testing` green; zero warnings in touched files.
- Serial run of both suites: **37/37** in 32.6 s.
- Live gate (jb55): 1y 2025-09-19 → 2 events EOSE · 2y 2024-09-19 → 5 events EOSE · 3y 2023-09-19 → 3 events EOSE · total 10, cacheable, 10 s.
- pbxproj three-dot diff: none.

### Gates (GATE.md, HEAD)
1. hermetic serial on the box — expected the known four-failure set, no `NEW`
2. unit coverage for the four pure helpers — inside Gate 1
3. LIVE read-only — `MemoriesLiveTests` with the enable file; report the three `MEMORIES_LIVE window=` lines
4. by hand — teaser appears on both feeds, dismisses with Undo, stays dismissed for the day; drawer row opens the sheet
5. no pbxproj diff (three-dot)

### Related, filed not fixed here
- #86 — shared NIP-10 predicates (`hasThreadingETag` counts a bare `["e"]`, case-sensitive `mention`, six inline copies). Also answers whether the fix would make #4 pass: no.
- zapcooking/zap_cooking_android#258 — primal is a dead slot in Android's `ARCHIVE_RELAYS`.

title: Wisper 3.1.0: 22-language local models, live Bluetooth mics and lifetime stats
body:
## Wisper 3.1.0

Brings fully offline multilingual dictation, live Bluetooth microphones, and major reliability hardening. This is 100 commits ahead of `main` (3.0.0).

### Highlights
- **22 Indian languages offline** — AI4Bharat IndicConformer 600M Multi (~2.45 GB, 7 files) and local Whisper large-v3 int8 (~1.69 GB) alongside Parakeet and Moonshine. All run on-device via `ort`/`sherpa-onnx` with 6h model cache.
- **Live microphone picker** — enumerates `cpal::available_hosts()` (ALSA/PipeWire) so Bluetooth headsets appear while Wisper is running (`GeneralTab` polls 3s + focus + tray open). Shows correct `DeviceDescription::name`, keeps `bluez` nodes, handles I32/U32/F64 and suppresses ALSA Xrun spam.
- **Lifetime stats** — `Words`, `Avg Words`, `Time saved` are now lifetime totals stored in `settings.json` and never reset on `Clear history`. Only `Dictations` resets. One-time migration seeds from existing history.

### Models & Engine
- New catalog entries `indicconformer-600m-multi` and `whisper-large-v3-int8` with multi-file download, `is_model_complete` check and re-download of incomplete dirs. Priority-aware transcription: Whisper tries `enabled_languages` in pill order, 600M biases CTC logits.

### UI
- `GeneralTab`: draggable language pills (handle-only grab), searchable Select, single-column layout, mic `Refresh` and `— not found` fallback.
- `HistoryTab`: lifetime stats with tooltips, `AudioContext` closed in `finally`, paged history.
- `EngineTab`: explicit `cancelDownload(modelName)`, `formatModelFilename` covers all keys.

### Hardening
- Pipeline `PipelineGuard` + cancellation-aware `SEQ_TURN` (no deadlock on panic), `create_new(0o600)` for all wavs with Windows retry, `is_model_complete` for partial downloads, `clear_history` OOM fix, `SILENCE_LOCK` for `silence_stderr`, `tray` cached tooltip.
- Paste: `Enigo` retry without holding lock, clipboard 30 ms Wayland delay.
- Process: deduped `build_body`/`parse_content` for sync/async.
- `App`: queued `saveSetting`/`saveAllSettings` via `saveQueueRef`, `refreshCurrentModel` inside queue.
- Security: tighten `tauri.conf.json` `connect-src` but keep `https: wss:` for custom providers.

### Docs
- Showcase redesigned as Linux terminal demo with correct 156×44 pill and beam.

### Testing
- `cargo check`/`cargo test` (4 passed)/`pnpm build` pass. Manual: Bluetooth hotplug, clear history, paste, overlay.

### Added since PR opened
- `6cc7e66` `fix(engine): correct IndicConformer 600M input names` — `engine.rs:808` `features`/`features_lens` and `engine.rs:830` `encoded` fix `encoder run: Invalid input name: audio_signal`
- `50a3a6b` `fix(ci): update release workflow for Ubuntu 24.04 and Tauri v2` — `release.yml:28` `libayatana-appindicator3-dev` + `libsoup-3.0-dev`, `release.yml:53` `@v1`→`@v2`
